activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Leo had told his mother he didn't need help, which was true in the way that most of his confident statements were true, which was to say he believed them hardest right before they failed. The community kitchen on Alder Street was empty on Sunday afternoons except for Ms. Cheung, who ran the place and let him use the big six-burner range because his own house had a stove that worked the way an old dog walked, reluctantly and in short distances. His mother was working the late shift. His grandmother, who had cooked for the family every Sunday of Leo's childhood, had been in the hospital since March, and the task of Sunday dinner had settled on him the way weather settles, without anyone deciding.

He set out the chicken thighs the way his grandmother used to: salt, nothing else, because she had claimed that anything more was showing off. He put a pan on the burner, added a splash of water, laid the thighs in, and clamped on a lid. Steaming seemed gentler, more forgiving, and he needed forgiveness from this meal. Kayleb and Jayden had come along, ostensibly to help, actually because Kayleb's house was loud and Jayden's was worse. They sat on the steel counter by the window passing a phone back and forth.

Forty minutes later Leo lifted the lid. The chicken had turned an even, unappetizing grey, pale as something drowned, sitting in its own thin liquid. Steam curled up and vanished. He had never in his life been embarrassed in front of Kayleb, and he wasn't now, though he turned the pot so the window was behind him and said, "It's basically the same, it just needs the sauce."

Jayden slid off the counter and looked. "Leo. That's the color of a rainy Tuesday."

"I know what I'm doing," Leo said, and did not. He poked a thigh with a fork and thought of his grandmother's drumsticks, lacquered and brown, the skin crisp enough to shatter under a tooth. Something atavistic in him wanted that crust, wanted the smell of it the way a person wants a room they grew up in. He stood there with the fork dripping.

Ms. Cheung came over from the office with a clipboard she wasn't reading. She didn't lecture; she had told him once that a kitchen was a small polity and everyone in it deserved a vote, and that his vote had elected a steamed bird. She asked if his grandmother had written anything down.

There was a shoebox. He had brought it, though he'd told Kayleb it was just stuff, nothing important, and Kayleb had wisely said nothing. Inside were recipe cards in his grandmother's cramped hand, and near the bottom, a card with no recipe at all. Just a sentence in pencil, pressed hard: "The pan must be hot first. The Maillard reaction, between the amino acids and the sugars, is what browns the food and makes most of the flavor, and it goes fast at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius. Steam is nothing. Heat the pan dry."

"She knew that word?" Kayleb said, holding the card near the window light. "The Maillard reaction. Your grandmother was out here studying chemistry."

"She knew everything," Leo said. "She just pretended she didn't." He wiped the thighs dry with paper towel, poured the grey liquid down the drain, and set the empty pan back on the burner. He cranked it high and waited, doing nothing, which was the hardest part. Jayden held his hand above the steel until he couldn't hold it anymore, and said, "That's got to be past 165 by now," and Leo turned it down a notch, not because he was sure but because the card had said fast, and fast meant there was such a thing as too much.

When the thighs hit the dry pan, the sound was a hiss like rain on a hot road, and within a minute the edges of the skin went gold, then amber, then a deep brown that seemed to transmute the bird into something from a different, better world. The smell filled the kitchen and two of the Sunday volunteers drifted over asking what it was. Leo didn't say, because it was his grandmother's, though he had not cried once since March, not at the hospital and not here, and his eyes were dry now too, whatever Jayden would later claim.

They ate at the long communal table off paper plates, the four of them and Ms. Cheung and one of the volunteers, tearing the chicken with their hands. Kayleb went back for seconds, then thirds, and said, "Do it exactly like this next week," and Leo said, "I invented it," and nobody believed him, and it didn't matter. There was a second batch in the pan, already browning, and Jayden leaned over it, breathing in the smoke. "One sixty-five," he said. "Right there. Right there."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he murdered an old man.
story:
The essay prompt sat on the kitchen table beside a mug of tea gone cold, and Sierra had read it eleven times. Ms. Bouchard wanted eight hundred words on how a narrator's point of view shapes what the reader believes, using an example of her choosing, and Sierra had chosen Poe because it was short and because she'd assumed it would be easy. It was not easy. It was two in the afternoon on a Sunday, her mother was at work until eleven, and the paragraph she had typed so far said that the narrator of "The Tell-Tale Heart" was creepy, which was true and useless.

She texted Fatoumata first, then Katerina, then set the phone face down to forestall any further checking of it. Both of them were doing the same essay. Katerina replied within a minute: coming over, bringing the book, don't start without me. Fatoumata's reply came slower, and it said only, can I come too, my house is loud today. Sierra read it twice. Fatoumata's house was never loud; Fatoumata was the one who texted in full sentences and never used exclamation points. She wrote back, yes, door's open, and then, because she was the one who noticed these things, she cleared the table of her own mess, put out three glasses, and found the packet of biscuits Katerina liked, the ones with the dark chocolate.

They arrived within ten minutes of each other, Katerina with her copy of the story bristling with sticky notes, Fatoumata with nothing but her bus pass and a look Sierra pretended not to catalog. "Okay," Katerina said, dropping into the chair across from Sierra. "My whole problem is I believe him. Which is embarrassing. He killed a man and hid the pieces under the floorboards and I still, when I read it, half believe he's calm."

"Why do you believe him?" Sierra asked.

"Because he says so? He keeps saying he's not mad. Over and over."

Fatoumata, who had taken the biscuit Sierra slid toward her without being offered twice, looked up. "That's the thing, though. That's what got me. The narrator keeps insisting he's not mad while he's describing how he murdered the old man. All the protests. That's exactly when I stopped trusting him." She said it almost apologetically, as though she were interrupting, and then reached for her tea.

Sierra sat back. The three of them were quiet for a moment, the radiator ticking, a neighbour's dog barking somewhere down the street. "Say that again," she said.

"The protests are the problem. If he really were sane, he wouldn't need to keep telling me."

Sierra pulled the laptop toward her and deleted creepy. What if the doubt wasn't in spite of what the narrator said but because of it? The story was a confession, first person, every detail filtered through a mind that called itself careful, that called its own nervousness sharpened senses, that heard the dead man's heart and attributed the sound to his own anxiety. The reader couldn't verify anything. There was only the voice, and the voice was busiest defending itself. "He's not just unreliable," she said slowly, typing as she spoke. "The point of view makes him unreliable. Like, we only get the murder through him. So the thing we'd use to judge him is the thing that's broken."

"That's the essay," Katerina said. "That's literally the whole essay."

But Sierra was already doubting it, the way she had learned to doubt anything that arrived too neatly. She turned the idea over. If protesting sanity made readers suspicious, then what did that mean for any first-person account? Her own college application essay, the one she'd polished until it shone, all admissions and obstacles overcome, was it trustworthy in the way she intended, or was the shine itself the tell? She said some of this out loud and Fatoumata laughed, softly, into her glass.

"You're doing the thing," Fatoumata said. "The thing where you take it too far."

"I'm taking it the right amount far. The essay has to go somewhere. It can't just be about one story."

"Then go somewhere honest," Katerina said. "Say you don't know where the line is. Say the reader's trust gets built and broken by the same words and you can't fully separate them." She was flipping through her sticky notes, and she paused on one near the end. "He hears the heart under the floorboards. Or he says he does. There's no way to check. That's your counterpoint, right there. He sounds certain, and certainty is all we get, and certainty is worthless."

Fatoumata set down her glass. "Or it isn't," she said. "Because I believed my grandmother when she said she was fine, and she was fine, for two more years. People who say they're fine aren't always lying." Her voice was even, but Sierra caught the small tremor under it, some subterranean current Fatoumata was keeping below the surface on purpose, and she reached over and refilled the glass without a word, and Fatoumata's hand rested for a second on her wrist and then withdrew.

They wrote until the light went amber and then grey. Sierra's essay ended with a question she couldn't answer: whether a narrator who insists on his own sanity has told the reader anything at all. She read it aloud to them, and Katerina nodded, and Fatoumata said it was good, and none of them said whether that was the truth. At the door, holding her book, Katerina turned back. "Tomorrow, before class, read us the last paragraph again. If we believe you, you're fine."

"Is that a compliment?" Sierra asked.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The campus tour began under an oak tree whose roots had cracked the brick walkway into small mountain ranges, and Thomas stood at the back of the group with his hands in his pockets, counting how many times the guide said the word "community." He was here because his mother had driven four hours and refused to let him stay home and refresh his application portal instead. The answer from this college could come any day. He had applied early, been deferred, and now the ordinary decision pool would judge him all over again, which felt like being made to re-audition for a part he had already failed to get.

Savana elbowed him when the guide, a senior in a green polo, stopped in front of the library and began to gesticulate at the clock tower as though introducing a relative. "This place changed my life," the guide said, which was the kind of thing Thomas distrusted on principle. Savana, though, was writing it all down. She wanted this school the way other people wanted specific concert tickets. Parker had come along for the cafeteria and said so openly, and was currently photographing a squirrel.

Then, near the admissions building, the guide said the thing Thomas would think about for the rest of the day. "And I'll just brag for a second, because you all applied to a school with one of the highest yield rates in the country." A father near the front raised his hand. "What's yield?"

The guide smiled like someone who had been asked this at every tour for four years. "Yield is the percentage of students we admit who then accept the offer and enroll."

Thomas heard the words and felt something shift, small and specific, like a door easing open a crack. He had spent months thinking of admissions as a verdict on him, a number with his name on it. But this was a number with the college's name on it. The school was also waiting for an answer. The school also counted the days. Somewhere in that building, someone tracked whether the offers they sent out came back accepted, and worried, or at least measured, the gap.

He hung back as the group moved toward the dorms. "Can I ask something?" he said to the guide, catching up. "Does yield change how admissions works? Like, do they think about whether you'll actually say yes?" The guide's smile went from rehearsed to real. "That's a good question. Ask me again when you're a senior doing this job." Not an answer, but not a door closing either.

He found Savana and Parker at the fountain, and told them what he'd worked out walking over: that deferral might not be a rejection, that the college had reasons to keep its options open too, the same way he was keeping his. Parker lay on the fountain's rim with his eyes closed. "So you're saying the college got rejected by people too, basically." "I'm saying it's not just them choosing," Thomas said. "It's both ways, all the way down." Savana looked at him, then at the admissions building, then said quietly, "I never thought of it like that. I've been writing them essays like I'm asking forgiveness."

The three of them got sandwiches, and Thomas, who had spent the drive being a gratuitous pessimist about his chances, announced he was done with that. "I've decided I'm allowed to want this without pretending I don't care," he said. "And I'm allowed to be wrong about getting in without it meaning I was wrong to want it." Parker toasted him with a lemonade. Savana said that was the most sense he'd made since junior year.

On the walk back to the car, his mother asked how it went, and instead of shrugging Thomas told her about yield, about the two-way street of it, about how the deferment letter had stopped feeling like a scarlet letter. She didn't say anything for a block, and then she said, "So you'd go if they take you." "If," he said. "But yeah. If."

That night, back home, he opened his laptop and, instead of refreshing the portal, wrote a short letter to the regional admissions officer, the one who had signed the deferral, saying he remained interested and enclosing nothing dramatic, just a paragraph about the tour and a question about the engineering program that the website hadn't answered. It took forty minutes to get the tone right. He read it once more, decided it was honest, and pressed send.

Then he closed the laptop, put it in his backpack for the morning, and went to find his mother to tell her the thing about the clock tower, the way the guide had pointed at it like a proud uncle, a real raconteur, the kind of person who could make even a building sound like it had said yes.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Jeremy had told her the skating rink at seven, and now it was six forty and he was standing at the rental counter counting his money like a man auditing a small, embarrassing fortune. Twelve dollars and some change. The cashier watched him with the patience of someone who had seen a hundred indigent teenagers probe their pockets for skate money, and Jeremy, deciding against the hot chocolate, pushed the bills across.

"You're going to fall," said Zachariah, who had insisted on coming early to watch, the way you might attend a friend's surgery. "You're going to fall, and she's going to skate a slow, dignified circle around your body."

"I took lessons when I was nine." It came out more defensive than he intended, but it was true, mostly true. He could still remember the flash of it: the indoor rink by his old school, the smell of cold rubber and disinfectant, an instructor named Mr. Van Dijk who used to cajole the wobblers off the wall with promises of juice, his gloved hand out like a crossing guard. "Falling is a skill," Mr. Van Dijk had said back then, demonstrating with theatrical dignity, folding to the ice and sitting there a moment before rising in one motion. "Learn to do it well and you will never fear it." Jeremy had loved him precisely because he made falling seem planned.

That was nine years ago and the ice tonight felt different, faster under his blades, the arena loud with music and the hiss of a hundred edges. He was on his fourth lap, testing himself, when Rayhan found him at the boards.

"She's here," Rayhan said. "Blue coat. Also, I need you to settle something, because Zachariah is being a coward about it."

"I'm being sensible," Zachariah called from the bench where he was lacing his skates with the deliberation of a bomb technician. "There's a psych thing. My sister took the course. In 1974, two researchers, Dutton and Aron, did a study where men crossed a scary suspension bridge, and after that they were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge. She wrote it on my arm."

"Called her," Rayhan said. "That's the whole point. They called her, after. More of the scared ones called."

"Right. So," Zachariah said, standing, wobbling, gripping the boards, "my question is this. If you take a girl to a horror movie and her heart is pounding, how do you know if it's you or the movie? What if the whole thing is fake? What if love is just fear with better lighting?"

"That's not what the study says," Rayhan said. "It says the scared bridge men called more. It doesn't say why. My sister says nobody in psychology agrees on why anything."

They argued the point around one slow lap, Zachariah trailing both hands along the rail like a man arrested by the rink itself, and Jeremy listened with half an ear because the other half had spotted the blue coat. Her name was Priya in his mind all week, though of course it was actually Priya, he had not hallucinated that part, and she was lacing her skates with quick, sure tugs that suggested competence. His stomach performed something structural.

"Go," Rayhan said. "Be frightened. Get confused about your own heartbeat. It's practically science."

She was better than him, which he learned in the first thirty seconds when she passed him backward, teasing, her breath a small cloud. He laughed and tried to chase her and his blade caught a rut and the world tipped. He fell the way Mr. Van Dijk had taught him, loose and low, and sat on the ice looking up at the fluorescent lights while she spun back to him, worried, hovering.

"Are you okay?"

"Falling is a skill," he said from the floor. "I planned that."

She laughed, which was worth the bruise, and pulled him up, and her mittened hand was warm even through the wool, and his heart was hammering now from the fall and from the laugh and from the blue coat close enough to smell, something like orange peel. There it was, the exact problem Zachariah had raised, sitting in his chest like an exam question. Pounding heart. Attractive person. No control group. He could not tell which part was the ice and which part was her, and he understood suddenly that the men on the scary bridge in 1974 had probably not known either, that the not knowing might just be what the beginning felt like, the two sources indistinguishable until, maybe, later, on some calm and sturdy bridge of an ordinary Tuesday, you still wanted to call.

"I have to tell you something embarrassing," Priya said as they glided into the far turn. "I've never seen anyone fall that gracefully."

"That's not embarrassing."

"Fine. My embarrassing thing is I told my friends this was a study date, because I couldn't tell if it was a date date, and if you say it's not, I'm moving to the far end of the rink and becoming a hermit."

Across the ice, Zachariah had let go of the boards and was gliding, actually gliding, arms out like a plutocrat surveying lands that were finally his. Jeremy watched him nearly collide with a six-year-old, correct, and bow.

"It's a date date," Jeremy said. "And possibly an experiment."

"Then hold on," she said, and pulled him into the fast lane, and his heart, hopeless and honest, kept no records at all.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Canada's federal Goods and Services Tax, introduced on January 1, 1991 at 7 percent, has been 5 percent since January 1, 2008.
story:
Victoria opened the spreadsheet she had been avoiding for a week and typed the number at the top of her first paycheque stub: 412.68. Below it, in smaller print, the stub itemized what the employer had withheld: income tax, CPP, EI. She subtracted them in the spreadsheet and arrived at a figure that matched the net pay line exactly, which pleased her more than she expected. Gross minus deductions, she wrote in the next cell, and then deleted it, because it looked like something a textbook would say.

She was saving for a laptop, and the laptop cost $849.99. At her Saturday job at the hardware store she had learned to ring up a receipt with one hand while counting change with the other, and she had noticed that the register added a line marked GST at the bottom of every sale. Five percent. A customer buying a $40 drill paid forty dollars and two dollars more, and the two dollars did not belong to the store or to her.

That was where her mother's old receipts came in. Her mother kept everything in a shoebox, and tonight Victoria had carried the box to her desk beside the computer, because she had a plan: she would add up what her family had paid in sales tax over the years, out of curiosity, and also because the number felt like something she ought to know. The oldest receipt in the box was from a restaurant, dated March 1991, curled at the corners, the ink gone brown. Its tax line was different. Seven percent.

She sat with that for a moment. Seven percent in 1991, five percent on the receipts she printed at work. Somewhere between those two dates the rate had changed, and she wanted to know exactly where, so she opened the browser and typed the question in plain words. The answer came back plainly enough: the Goods and Services Tax had taken effect on January 1, 1991, at 7 percent, and had been 5 percent since January 1, 2008. She read it twice, then copied both dates into her spreadsheet, one beside each receipt.

Her phone buzzed. It was Marina, who had heard from Sidney that Victoria was doing a tax return, and Marina wanted to know whether it was true that you could get money back. Victoria typed that yes, sometimes, if your employer had withheld more income tax than you ended up owing, the return was how you got the difference back. Marina replied that the whole system sounded like an artifice, a maze built to confuse people into paying twice, and Victoria laughed, then stopped laughing, because she could not entirely argue. She had spent forty minutes tonight learning to read a single slip of paper.

At the store, the next Saturday, the subtext arrived wearing a work jacket. An older man, Mr. Virtanen from two streets over, laid a receipt on the counter and said, quietly, that the register had charged him tax on a bag of screws. Victoria looked at the receipt. The GST line sat at the bottom, five percent, correct as far as she could tell. He kept his finger on the paper and did not push it toward her, and she understood that he was not really asking about screws; he was asking whether the machine could be trusted, whether someone behind the counter would check rather than shrug. She re-added the totals out loud, line by line, and told him the amount was right. He studied her face for a second longer than the arithmetic required, then folded the receipt and put it in his pocket.

"Heard you lambaste the government the other day," she said, because Sidney had repeated it, and Mr. Virtanen smiled without apologizing. "Somebody should," he said. She thought of the 1991 receipt in the shoebox, seven percent, and of her mother paying it without comment at a restaurant twenty-some years before Victoria was born. There was something almost comforting in the arithmetic being legible, even when you disagreed with it. Not fair, exactly. Legible.

That evening she finished the spreadsheet and opened the tax return software her mother had left installed on the computer. It asked her questions in small grey boxes, and she answered them, and when it produced the result, a modest refund, she did not celebrate. She saved the file, wrote the laptop fund's new total on a sticky note, and pressed it to the monitor's edge. Then she took the 1991 receipt, flattened it under the heaviest book she owned, and left it there.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
Charlotte found the guitar in the hall closet behind the winter coats, a half-size classical her father had bought in a fit of ambition years ago and never touched again. The strings were dull and the third one buzzed when she pressed it, but when she sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor that first evening and dragged a thumb across them, the sound was warm and hollow at once, like a voice through a wall. She wanted to play one song, all the way through, at the spring showcase in five weeks. She had wanted something like that for a long time without ever saying it out loud.

At school the next day, Bronwyn laughed, not unkindly, when Charlotte told her. "You're sixteen," Bronwyn said, stacking her books. "It's basically pointless to start guitar at seventeen, even. Didn't you hear about that? Ten thousand hours. That's what it takes to get good at anything. You'd have to practice, like, four hours a day for a decade."

"That can't be right," Charlotte said, but the number followed her home. Ten thousand hours. She did the math on the back of a science worksheet and the answer was ugly.

Her neighbor Ms. Fortin had a shelf of books she lent out without ceremony, and among them Charlotte found a fat orange paperback with a cracked spine. Outliers, by Malcolm Gladwell. She read it at the kitchen table while her mother made tea, and there it was, the ten thousand hours, laid out like a law of nature. So Bronwyn had the number from somewhere real.

But a few nights later, chasing a footnote through a search on her laptop, she found something else. Gladwell's 2008 book had popularized the rule, but the researcher whose work it came from, a man named Ericsson, had later said the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Charlotte read the sentence twice, then closed the laptop and looked at the guitar leaning against her bed frame. Ten thousand hours was a door slamming. Quality of practice was a door left open a crack, and she could not tell, honestly, whether that crack was wide enough for her.

She practiced anyway. Her fingertips hurt in a specific way, sore at the very tips where the strings pressed ridges into the skin, and her left hand kept inventing reasons to quit: the stretch to the fifth fret, the curve of a barre chord that collapsed every time. Her mother knocked once to ask if she was strangling a cat. Charlotte laughed, which broke her concentration, and she had to begin the phrase again.

Jean, who had played violin since she was seven, came over on a Sunday and watched Charlotte attempt the same eight bars for twenty minutes. "You keep starting from the top," Jean said. "Every time you mess up, you go back to the beginning and play the part you already know."

"That's practicing," Charlotte said.

"That's performing for your bedroom." Jean took the guitar, badly, and plucked out the difficult two measures at half speed, again and again, until Charlotte took it back, annoyed and a little grateful. Afterward she tried it Jean's way: small chunks, slow, hands staying relaxed, fixing one thing at a time. It felt like suture work, stitching the phrase to itself a few threads at a time instead of trying to close the whole wound at once. It was tedious. It was also, by Thursday, working.

When she told Bronwyn about Ericsson, Bronwyn shrugged. "So you found a loophole."

"It's not a loophole. It's more like, the number was equivocal all along. Gladwell made it famous, and it's true he was going off real research, but the researcher himself backed off from it later. He said hours aren't the point."

"That sounds like pedantry," Bronwyn said, but she said it lightly, and when Charlotte played her the eight bars, slow but clean, Bronwyn stopped stacking her books to listen.

The showcase was on a Friday, and by Wednesday Charlotte still had not decided whether to sign up. Her fingertips had hardened into small calluses she kept running over with her thumb, a strange pride. The song was not good, exactly. It was simple, and there was a sloppy transition in the bridge where her hands still panicked. She could play it for her bedroom, or she could play it badly for a gymnasium. Those were different skills, and five weeks had only been enough time to get decent at one of them.

She sat on her bed Thursday night with the sign-up form on her desk and the guitar on her lap. Ms. Fortin had told her once, over returned books, that she had sung in choirs her whole life and only started piano at fifty. Charlotte had assumed she was being encouraged. Now she wondered if it was more complicated than that, if Ms. Fortin was also telling her something about the price: all those years of one instrument, and the second one arriving late, and whatever unnamed arithmetic lived underneath that choice.

The form required a name, an instrument, and one sentence about the performance. Charlotte wrote her name. Under instrument she wrote "guitar," and under the description, after a long pause, she wrote "one song, imperfectly." Her mother found her in the kitchen afterward, heating milk in a pan.

"You're doing it then," her mother said.

"Tomorrow. Six o'clock." Charlotte stirred the milk. "Bronwyn thinks I'll embarrass myself."

"And what do you think?"

"I think the hours are wrong," Charlotte said. "I mean the rule is wrong, or anyway it's not the whole thing. Ericsson said quality matters more, and he's the one who did the research, so." She tasted the milk. "But I don't actually know if I've practiced well enough. That part you can't look up."

In the morning she packed the guitar in a padded bag borrowed from Jean, the zipper sticking at the corner, and walked to school with it bumping against her hip. In the gymnasium at six, under lights that smelled faintly of dust, she unzipped the case, sat on the folding chair, and set her left hand on the strings.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Paul Graham's 2008 essay 'How to Disagree' ranks disagreement in seven levels, from name-calling at the bottom to refuting the other person's central point at the top.
story:
The co-op placement had put Faith at a small nonprofit office above a pharmacy, where she answered the phone, filed grant paperwork, and learned from Mr. Buchanan that a professional email begins with the reader's question, not the writer's grievance. She had been there three weeks when her phone buzzed all through Friday afternoon with the group chat for the student volunteer committee. The spring river cleanup was collapsing in public. Eve-Marie wanted a second date added for students who worked Saturdays; Graham called the suggestion "corporate nonsense," then something worse, and by evening someone had typed a word that made Faith's stomach drop, aimed at Eve-Marie herself.

She sat at the front desk after five, the office empty except for the hum of the radiator, scrolling backward through the thread the way you might study the scene of an accident. It hadn't started badly. It had started with a schedule and a budget, actual numbers, and it had decayed, message by message, until nobody was arguing about the event anymore. What mesmerized her was the pattern itself, so regular it seemed almost biological, as if the conversation had a homeostasis of its own: push it toward insult and it settled there, push it toward the schedule and it drifted back down.

Mr. Buchanan came out of his office with his coat already on and paused at the sight of her face. "Trouble at home, or trouble here?"

"Neither, kind of." She held up the phone. "My friends are fighting about our cleanup day and it turned into name-calling. I have to write the reply and I don't know how to say the thing that matters without sounding like I'm taking sides."

He considered that for a moment, then nodded at her screen. "Write it here Monday morning, on the clock, like it's a memo. You'll write better." And he left, which she understood, later, to be the entire lesson.

That night she went looking for how to argue without the rot setting in, half expecting to find nothing but listicles. Instead she landed on an essay by Paul Graham, from 2008, called "How to Disagree." She read it twice, then copied a line into her notebook. Graham ranked disagreement in levels, seven of them, with name-calling at the very bottom and, at the top, refuting the other person's central point. Between those poles lay everything she had watched happen in the chat, in order, as if he'd seen it coming.

On Monday she drafted the message at the office, structured the way Mr. Buchanan had taught her: a subject line that named the decision, one short paragraph of context, and then the disagreement itself, aimed at Graham's argument and not at Graham. She wrote that Eve-Marie's central point, that Saturday workers were being excluded, stood unrefuted, and that no one had yet answered it. She wrote that the insults ranked at the bottom of the ladder and the schedule question sat at the top, and that the committee was welcome to climb. Then she deleted the sentence about climbing, because it sounded smug, and put the ladder's levels in a footnote instead. She showed the draft to Mr. Buchanan. He read it without expression, which she had learned was his highest praise, and said only, "Send it."

The chat went quiet for most of an hour. Then Eve-Marie replied with a single line of thanks, and Graham, to Faith's genuine surprise, wrote a longer message admitting he'd been out of line, though he still thought the budget couldn't stretch to a second date, and here were three reasons why, laid out in numbered form, which was more structure than Graham had ever shown in his life. He had not become agreeable. He had become refutable, which turned out to be the more useful condition. By Wednesday the committee had voted on a compromise: one Saturday event, with a Sunday shift that Graham himself offered to coordinate, since, as he put it, "apparently I care more than I thought."

What stayed unresolved, in Faith's mind, was the boy who had typed the cruel word and never returned to the chat. She didn't know whether the ladder reached people who wouldn't climb it at all, and the essay, as far as she could tell, didn't say. She printed the final schedule from the office printer on her last Friday, folded it, and took it to the pharmacy counter downstairs, where he worked the register. She set it on the belt between his scanner and the gum display.

"We start Sunday at nine," she said. "If you want it, it's yours."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Jains, Sikhs and some Buddhists, families light small oil lamps called diyas in homes and temples to symbolize light overcoming darkness.
story:
Joshua's mother had him count the cotton wicks twice, and both times he came up with forty-one, which was a number that meant nothing to him and seemed to bother her not at all. The kitchen smelled of cardamom and frying something, and his aunt was expostulating from the doorway about the state of the front step, which had not been swept, which was, according to her, a matter of family reputation and possibly civilization itself.

"You're on diya duty," his mother said, pressing the small clay lamps into his hands like a verdict. "Rows along the walkway, both sides, before seven."

He carried the box outside and set it down on the cold porch. The lamps were plain little bowls of terracotta, each one shallow enough to hold a thumb of oil. His cousin had done this job last year, and the year before, and Joshua had watched from the window both times, aware that he was watching, aware that watching was a kind of answer to a question nobody had asked him. This year his cousin was at university in another province, and the box of lamps had landed on Joshua as if by gravity.

He knelt on the walkway and began. The concrete was damp from the afternoon rain, and the first lamp sat crooked until he wedged a pebble under its base. He tried spacing them evenly at first, measuring with his hand, but by the sixth lamp he'd stopped being precise about it and started noticing instead: how the wet concrete darkened the clay, how the oil trembled in each bowl when a car passed on the street. He wondered whether anyone had ever done this in the rain, on some flattened stretch of ground far from here, whether the lamps had guttered or whether the point was to set them out anyway.

Aubree texted him a photo from her own kitchen, where her family was doing nothing in particular, her caption reading "what are you actually doing tonight." He sent back a picture of the row of diyas and then, because a picture of unlit lamps told her nothing, he added: hindus, jains, sikhs and some buddhists celebrate this, it's called diwali, you light the little oil lamps at home and in temples. Light over darkness. He looked at what he'd typed and wondered where he'd learned it. Not from his mother, exactly, who preferred doing to explaining. From the internet, probably, or from overhearing his aunt at some earlier party, the words absorbed the way you absorb the floor plan of a house you grew up in.

Darwin arrived at seven-fifteen with a paper bag of something his own grandmother had made, because Darwin's family was Christian but lived three doors down and had long ago stopped treating the difference as a wall. He stood at the end of the walkway with his hands in his pockets, surveying the two rows of lamps like a man considering a bridge.

"Are they supposed to be straight?" Darwin said.

"They're supposed to be lit."

"That's a better answer than straight."

Joshua had a book of matches in his pocket, the long wooden kind, and he'd been putting off the lighting because once he started it would be real, a commitment to the whole arrangement. He crouched at the far end, touched a flame to the first wick, and watched it catch with a small orange sound. He moved down the row. Each flame was a separate decision, and by the tenth he'd stopped deciding and was just moving, and by the twentieth the light was doing something to the walkway that he hadn't expected, turning the ordinary concrete into a surface with gold in it.

Ms. Carvalho from across the street came out to collect her recycling and stopped at her curb. She was his retired English teacher from two years ago, a woman who had once told him that an essay was a lamp you set down wherever the reader was standing. She looked at the rows of flames for a long moment.

"It looks like a runway," she said.

"It's not going anywhere."

"Neither is a runway. That's rather the point of one."

Guests began arriving at half past seven, an uncle first, then neighbours with foil-covered dishes, and the walkway with its two burning lines did its work on all of them, slowing their steps, lowering their voices. Joshua stood near the door handing out the little paper plates his mother had stacked for him, and he found himself watching faces as people passed the flames, wondering whether the lamps meant the same thing to his aunt, who had grown up with them, as they did to Darwin, who was seeing them for the first time, as they did to him, who was somewhere in the middle and not sure the middle was a real place. Light overcoming darkness. He understood the words. He was less sure he understood what his own darkness was supposed to be, or whether naming it was germane, or whether some things did their work without being named, the way the lamp did its work without understanding oil.

His aunt found him at the door and put a hand on his shoulder. "Forty-one," she said, as though continuing an argument with the number. "Your grandmother used to do one hundred and eight. She'd run out of room and put them on the windowsills."

"Why one hundred and eight?"

His aunt considered this. "Because she had one hundred and eight," she said, and went inside.

Later, when the guests were loud in the kitchen and the smell of frying had given way to the smell of burnt sugar, Joshua walked back down the walkway alone. One lamp near the end had gone out, its wick black and its oil still full. He struck a match, cupped it, and touched it to the wick, and the flame came back uncertain, then steady. He stayed crouched there longer than the task required, holding the match until it burned down to his fingers.

"You'll burn yourself," Darwin called from the porch.

"I know," Joshua said, and shook the match out.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
story:
The chemistry exhibit on the third floor of the science museum had a inflated plastic cube the size of a small car parked near the window, and Kate circled it twice before she trusted herself to read the card. "One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure," said a voice behind her, and Rayan appeared, holding a cone of fries he had smuggled up from the cafeteria despite three separate signs forbidding it. He tapped the cube. "This thing is supposed to be that much space, more or less. Twenty-two point four litres. They vilify me for the fries but they let this monstrosity loose on children."

"It's not that big," Kate said, but she was already doing the arithmetic in her head, or trying to. A mole of water was eighteen grams, she knew that, and a mole of hydrogen gas was two grams, which meant two grams of the stuff would fill this whole ridiculous cube if you kept it cold. Two grams. A raisin weighed more than that. She said so, and Daphne, arriving with the calm of someone who had spent the bus ride memorising nothing, said, "That's the point of the exhibit, you realise. You're having the intended reaction. Congratulations, you're the demo."

The problem, the actual problem, was the worksheet Ms. Rahman had handed out that morning on the museum steps, the one due Monday, the one Kate had been avoiding through two floors of optical illusions. "Calculate the moles of oxygen produced from 32.0 grams of hydrogen peroxide," it said, and then, more menacingly, "then state the volume the gas would occupy." The molar masses were printed in a table at the bottom like fine print on a contract. Kate had glared at it over lunch. Daphne had offered to walk her through it and Kate had said no, too quickly, because the truth was she wanted to get it herself, or at least to fail at it in private.

They sat down on the bench under the cube. Daphne produced a pen from her jacket like an auxiliary limb she kept for emergencies, and Kate laid the worksheet flat on her knee. "Hydrogen peroxide," she muttered. "H2O2. So the molar mass is..." She added on her fingers like a despot counting prisoners: two hydrogens, two oxygens. Two plus thirty-two. Thirty-four grams in a mole of the stuff. "So thirty-two grams of it is less than a mole. Thirty-two over thirty-four."

"Which is what, as a number?" Rayan said, around a fry.

"Shut up, I'm doing long division in my head, which is a skill my grandmother had and I have abandoned." She got 0.94, roughly, and then something clicked sideways, the way it did sometimes, half arithmetic and half picture. The hydrogen peroxide split into water and oxygen, two molecules of the first for every one of the second, so the moles of oxygen weren't the moles of peroxide, they were half of it, and she sat forward because she could suddenly see the whole thing laid out like a route on a map. Half of 0.94 was 0.47, and if one mole of gas took about 22.4 litres, cold, at normal pressure, then 0.47 of a mole took about 10.5 litres. A balloon and a half. All that from a film canister's worth of liquid. She checked it twice, got the same answer twice, which she had learned was not the same as being right but was better than nothing.

Here is what I could not stop thinking, sitting under that stupid glorious cube with the worksheet finally done: that my chemistry teacher had spent three weeks trying to hand me this and I had treated it like a foreign tax code, and then a plastic box and a smuggled cone of fries had done it in an afternoon. The numbers were the same numbers. Nothing about the method had changed. What changed was that I had wanted to know, suddenly, personally, how much room a raisin's worth of gas would take up, and the wanting was the whole difference.

"You look smug," Daphne said.

"I feel smug, which is different, and probably worse." I folded the worksheet into quarters. "I still don't get why it's 22.4 litres. Like, why that number and not a round one. Nobody's told me that part and I don't think the cube knows either." I kicked it, gently, and it wobbled with a slow rubbery dignity. Rayan held out the cone of fries, which was his version of a peace treaty, or a knighthood. I took one.

Ms. Rahman found them there ten minutes later, her lanyard swinging, her clipboard mercifully blank. "Done?" she asked, and Kate handed over the paper before she could lose her nerve. Ms. Rahman read it, and read it again, and her eyebrows did something Kate chose to interpret favourably. "The reasoning on the second part is sound," she said, which was as close to applause as she got. "Volume at the stated conditions. Good." Then, at the bottom of the page, in red: why 22.4? and a small arrow pointing at the margin, where she had drawn a box the size of a stamp with a question mark inside it.

Kate looked at the empty box for a long moment. "You want me to find that out too?"

"I want you to want to find that out," Ms. Rahman said, and walked off toward the elevator, tapping her pen against the clipboard in a rhythm Kate suspected was not accidental.

"She's a despot," Rayan said fondly, through the last fry.

"She's a despot with a point." Kate turned back to the cube, put her palm flat against the cool plastic, and felt it give slightly, as if the whole mole of nothing in there had shifted over to make room.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
Sofia had turned eighteen on the fourth of October, and the election came on the fifth of November, which felt less like a coincidence than a test of whether she deserved the timing. Her grandmother insisted on driving her to the community hall on Maple Street, a building Sofia knew only as the place where the scouting troops sold popcorn and where Mr. Karimi taught his Saturday citizenship class, the one Sofia had taken in the spring mostly because Jolie had signed them both up.

Inside, the hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Folding tables had been arranged into lanes, and behind each lane sat a pair of election workers with the patient, slightly bored posture of people who had been there since six. Jolie was already in line, camera hanging off her shoulder, waving with her whole arm.

"You're doing a whole documentary," Sofia said when she reached her.

"It's for the school archive," Jolie said. "First-time voters, 2024. I want the poll workers, the signage, your hands on the ballot. The aesthetic of a community hall voting." She adjusted her lens. "Nobody photographs this part. Just the stickers."

"You are, in your heart, an aesthete," Sofia said. "You'd film a drainage ditch if the light was right."

"I would," Jolie agreed, "and it would be beautiful."

The line moved in short shuffles. Ahead of them, an old man argued gently with a worker about which precinct he belonged to, and the worker walked him to a different table herself instead of pointing, one hand hovering near his elbow. Sofia watched her do it, and something in her recalibrated, her idea of the day loosening from ceremony toward something plainer and more durable.

Her grandmother had planted the whole thing at dinner the night before, over rice and lentils. "You know I couldn't vote at eighteen," she had said, spooning more onto Sofia's plate before Sofia asked for it, the way she always did. "None of us could. It was the Twenty-Sixth Amendment that changed it, 1971. Ratified in about three months. Faster than any other amendment."

"That fast?" Sofia had said.

"That fast," her grandmother said. "All those years, and then, in a hurry, suddenly." She had not explained why, and Sofia had not asked, partly because she suspected the answer was long and partly because her grandmother's face had gone somewhere private, and you did not interrupt that.

Now, at the front of the line, a worker with reading glasses on a beaded chain found Sofia's name in the register. "First time?" the woman asked, already reaching for the pen.

"First time."

"Sign here. Sweetheart, the booth's to your left." The booth was a canvas contraption on spindly legs, and the ballot slid into a slot that had clearly been designed for some earlier machine; the old lever mechanism was vestigial now, a chrome handle that no longer did anything but that no one had removed. Sofia pulled the curtain, stood in the small privacy of it, and read the ballot twice, because she had promised herself she would.

She had promised Coen, too, in a way. Coen had cornered her after Mr. Karimi's class in the spring and argued that a single vote in a national election was statistically meaningless, a ritual, and that she was romanticizing it. "Then rituals matter," Sofia had said at the time, not entirely sure she believed it. She had gone home and looked up the amendment herself, scrolling through the National Archives site on her phone, and found it exactly as her grandmother said: the voting age set at eighteen, 1971, about three months from proposal to ratification, faster than any other amendment. Faster than the ones that ended slavery, faster than the one that gave women the vote. Coen was right that her one ballot would not decide anything. Her grandmother was right that people had rushed, had pushed, so that eighteen-year-olds could do this thing that would not decide anything. Both of those were true at once, and Sofia could not make them cancel out, and she had stopped trying. She filled in the ovals with the stubby pencil, checking each one against the sample ballot in her pocket where she had written, in her own handwriting, the offices she cared about and the ones she was guessing on. There were more guesses than she wanted to admit.

She fed the ballot into the scanner, which swallowed it with a mechanical clunk, and turned to find Jolie already shooting, crouched low for the angle.

"Hands," Jolie said. "Give me your hands."

Sofia held them out, palms up, and Jolie took four frames, then lowered the camera. "Okay, now the sticker. Wear it somewhere visible, the archive needs it." She handed Sofia the roll of stickers she had begged off the poll worker, a whole roll, because Jolie never did anything by halves.

Sofia peeled one off and pressed it onto her jacket, crooked, and looked around for her grandmother, who was waiting by the coffee urn, holding two paper cups, one of them the wrong kind, decaf, the kind she always chose for Sofia without asking.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
Aidan had claimed the window seat on Sunday afternoon with a blanket, a thermos, and a photocopy of Chapter Twelve of Pride and Prejudice, because on Tuesday he had to present something called a feminist critical reading, and so far all he understood about it was that it existed. The nook smelled like dust and the cedar lining his mother had put in the bench years ago. He read the paragraph where Charlotte Lucas declares that happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance, and he read it again, and the margins stayed empty.

The problem was that he liked the book. He liked its wit and its pace, and every time he tried to look at it coldly, as a system instead of a story, he felt like a fraud, a boy holding a stolen instrument. He had underlined "I ask only a comfortable home," four words that Charlotte says with such efficiency, and beside them he had written, in pencil, because pencil could be apologized for, is she settling or is she rational.

Eloise arrived at four with her own copy and a bag of clementines, because she wanted to run her presentation past someone before Tuesday too. She wanted, she said as she folded herself into the corner of the nook, to argue that the novel punishes Charlotte for telling the truth, and she needed to know if that was defensible or just pugnacious. Aidan offered her the last of the thermos tea, which was mostly leaves, and she accepted it anyway.

"Charlotte's twenty-seven," Eloise said, peeling a clementine in one unbroken spiral, a trick she was quietly proud of. "Her family's embarrassed by her. If she doesn't marry Collins, she gets to be an aunt with a room in someone else's house."

"So it's a smart move," Aidan said. "That's what I keep landing on. She plays the only game available and she wins it."

"Then why does the book make you feel like she lost?"

He didn't have an answer, so he externalized the question instead, turning it outward the way Ms. Tanaka had told them to in the seminar on Tuesday. "What if we ask what the world around her wants women to want? Not what she wants. What she's been trained to want."

Eloise stopped peeling. "My mom has that book," she said. "The Second Sex. Simone de Beauvoir. It's on the shelf behind the piano with the other ones she bought in college and never reread." She was already texting her mother for permission to walk over and get it, which told Aidan the presentation mattered to her more than she had let on; she had a habit of burying stakes under jokes, and the absence of jokes now was itself information.

They walked the six blocks in the kind of cold that made conversation optional, and came back with the book, heavy and soft-covered, its spine cracked at several places. It took them twenty minutes of passing it back and forth to find the line, and when Eloise read it aloud she did it slowly, the way you read something that has been quoted at you your whole life without your knowing. "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." The book had come out in 1949, the copyright page said, and Aidan copied the date and the line into his notebook, checking each word twice.

"So Charlotte becomes," he said. "Everything she wants, she wants inside a fence. The comfortable home, the respectability, even the logic. The logic might be hers, but the fence isn't."

Eloise was quiet long enough that he worried he had said something wrong. Then she said, "That's the part I can't fix for Tuesday. If her wanting is trained, is any of it hers? I want to say her choices are real. I want to say she sees the board better than Elizabeth does. But if I say that, the lens says I'm excusing the board."

"That's not the lens losing," Aidan said. "That might be the lens working." He believed it as he said it, and he also believed its opposite, which was that a tool that only ever found the same answer was a hammer calling itself a microscope. He wrote both sentences down. Under the first he drew a small box, and inside the box he wrote "the fence," and then, after a pause, "who built it, who profits."

They worked until Eloise's phone buzzed with a ride home, and she stood in the entryway with the book hugged to her chest, borrowed for the week, her spiral of clementine peel still coiled on the arm of the nook like a small bright shell. At the door she turned back. "Present on the question, not the answer," she said. "Ms. Tanaka always says the thinking is the part."

After she left, Aidan sat in the window seat with the streetlight coming on outside and the notebook open on his knees. He read his box again, the fence, who built it, who profits, and beneath it he wrote a new line: Elizabeth refuses the fence and the novel rewards her with a fortune, which means the fence pays its refusers too, sometimes, if they're pretty enough and lucky. He looked at that for a while. He could build twelve minutes of talk out of it, or he could spend those minutes standing in front of the class admitting where the lens went dark on him.

He picked up the pencil, turned to a fresh page, and at the top wrote, "Where I'm still not sure."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Electric field strength can be measured in volts per metre or in newtons per coulomb, and the two units are equivalent.
story:
The bus parked in the lot behind the science museum just after ten, and Jesse filed in with the rest of Mr. Holloway's physics class, carrying the worksheet everyone was supposed to finish before lunch. The last question asked them to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates, and the museum had obligingly built an exhibit for exactly that: two brass plates a hand's width apart, a movable probe on a slider, and a readout that changed when you moved the probe along the line between them.

Jesse stationed himself at the slider while Zain copied the plate voltage off the placard and Breanna measured the gap with a ruler she had brought for no reason anyone could explain. The worksheet wanted them to parametrize the position of the point, so Jesse slid the probe in slow, even steps and called out the readings while Zain wrote them in a tidy column. The exhibit hummed, a low steady sound, and when Jesse put his hand near the housing the hum went quiescent, as though the thing were waiting to see what he would do next.

The arithmetic took them ten minutes. Zain divided the voltage by the separation and wrote his answer with a flourish: 150 volts per metre. Breanna, working from the force on a charge she had read off the placard, arrived at her own answer and set it down beside his: 150 newtons per coulomb.

"That's not what it asked," Zain said. "Look at the units. Mine are right."

"Mine are right," Breanna said. "Force per charge is what field strength is. You did it backwards."

They argued the way they argued about everything, without heat but without retreat, each holding a worksheet as evidence. Jesse listened and felt the familiar pull to take a side, the way he always had, back when arguments among his friends were about which method was faster and he had learned to champion whatever Zain was against. He had been, Breanna once told him, something of a revisionist about their ninth-grade lab reports, forever rewriting what they had concluded the night before it was due. He had not entirely stopped. But standing between the plates now, with two clean answers that disagreed only in their units, he found himself wanting something else.

He looked at the numbers again. Same value. Different units. He turned the worksheet over and wrote 150 V/m and then, beneath it, 150 N/C, and stared at the pair until Zain leaned over his shoulder.

"They can't both be right," Zain said.

"Unless the units are the same thing," Jesse said. "Volts per metre. Newtons per coulomb." He said it slowly, testing the shape of it, the way he tested a word in Spanish before using it on his grandmother. He did not know why it would be true, and he was careful not to pretend he did. He only knew the exhibit had given them one number and the two of them had come at it from opposite ends.

Breanna had already moved back to the slider. She set the probe at the point from the worksheet, watched the readout settle, and copied the number into the margin of her page without comment. Then she stepped aside and let Zain check it, and Zain read the display twice, once in silence and once aloud, and wrote his initials next to hers.

Mr. Holloway drifted over on his rounds, coffee cup in hand, and looked at the two answers side by side on the worksheet. He raised his eyebrows at Jesse and waited, in the way of a man who already knew what was on the page and wanted to see whether Jesse knew it too.

"We got the same number twice," Jesse said. "Volts per metre, newtons per coulomb. We think they're equivalent."

Mr. Holloway's mouth moved toward something like a smile, but he said only, "Mark that question finished, then," and moved on toward the plasma globe at the far end of the hall, where two other students were already arguing about something else.

Jesse slid the probe back and forth along the line between the plates one more time, watching the readout climb and fall, and he left both answers on the paper, units and all, side by side.

"Fifty says my units end up on the answer key," Zain said.

"No bet," said Breanna.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: German historian Alexander Demandt compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell.
story:
The argument started over the second plate of lamb, which was usual for Luca's family, though the subject was not. His uncle had read somewhere that Rome fell because of lead in the pipes, and he delivered this at the table the way other men discussed property prices. Luca's cousin's boyfriend, a graduate student called nothing but "the boyfriend" by everyone except Luca's aunt, set down his fork and said that was a pop explanation, that the real cause was structural overextension of the frontier. Between them sat Luca, seventeen, holding bread he was no longer eating.

He had a stake in this. Only two weeks earlier he had written a history essay arguing, with the conviction available only to someone who had just learned something, that Rome fell because of decadence, moral decay, the whole silhouette of it. Ms. Chowdhury had given it a B minus and a single comment in the margin: "Which sources are you leaning on, and which are leaning on you?" He had not fully understood the question, and it bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers a tongue.

"Decadence," said the uncle now, gesturing with the bread knife. "That's the one I was taught. They got soft."

"There's no serious scholarship behind softness," said the boyfriend, in the tone of a man disabusing a child about the tooth fairy. "You want economics, logistics, the shift in the tax base. Pick a real variable."

Luca's younger sister, who had been filming the argument for her own amusement, panned to Luca. "You did Rome this term," she said. "Tell them."

He could have said decadence. He had four paragraphs of it memorized, footnotes and all, and the uncle would have clapped his shoulder and the boyfriend would have looked superior and everyone would have gone back to the lamb. Instead he took out his phone, because he remembered something Kassandra had mentioned in the library two days ago while he was still smarting over the B minus. She had said the word "Demandt" and then been dragged off to a class, and he had written it on his hand.

"What are you doing," said the uncle.

"Hold on." The phone found it. "Alexander Demandt. A German historian. He compiled a list of all the different explanations writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell."

"How many?" the uncle asked, in the voice of a man humoring him.

"Two hundred and ten."

The boyfriend blinked. Luca watched him blink, and it was, privately, one of the better moments of his summer. "Two hundred and ten separate explanations," Luca went on, scrolling. "Lead pipes is on there. So is decadence. So is overextension, probably. Also bureaucracy, also weather, also some that are just strange."

"Some crank collected every bad theory and you're presenting it as evidence," the boyfriend said, but with less load-bearing certainty than before.

"He was counting what people have actually argued," Luca said. "That's the point. It's not that two hundred and nine people were idiots." He paused, aware he was now standing on the boyfriend's side of the argument and also somehow on the uncle's, which felt like standing in two boats. "It's that when you look back at a thing that big, every writer sees the part they came looking for. Lead was a nineteenth-century obsession. Decadence was the zeitgeist of whoever wrote your textbook, Uncle, because you went to school in a country that was nervous about getting soft." His uncle looked at him with an expression Luca filed under "wounded but intrigued."

The boyfriend said, "The sources are partial, yes, but method still sorts the strong claims from the weak ones. It's not a free-for-all."

"It's not a free-for-all," Luca agreed, "but it's also not a riddle with the answer on the last page. Ms. Chowdhury said something like that. Sort of." He had, in fact, just invented the second half, and he was honest enough with himself to note it: the essay's new draft, the one forming in his head, would concede that he had no way to adjudicate between lead and taxes and climate, only a way to describe why people kept choosing differently. That was a weaker position than his original one, and harder to argue, and he suspected it was the only defensible one. Angelina, when he'd complained about the grade, had said that being unsure was not the same as being vague, and he had not believed her until this table.

The uncle cut more lamb and put it on Luca's plate without being asked, which in their family was a form of concession. "So nobody knows why it fell."

"Two hundred and ten people thought they knew," Luca said.

His sister lowered the phone. "So what's yours? Number two hundred and eleven."

Luca looked at the lamb, then at his phone, then at the boyfriend, who was waiting with the particular stillness of a man hoping the seventeen-year-old would embarrass himself. "I think I'd want to know who was asking the question, and when, before I answered it," Luca said, and picked up his fork.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream's surface speed typically reaches about 2.5 metres per second at its fastest, making it one of the fastest ocean currents.
story:
The quarry had filled with rainwater decades ago, and the town had never decided whether it was a hazard or a swimming hole, so it remained both, ringed by a chain-link fence with a gap everyone knew about. Tyson spread the ocean current map on a flat slab of limestone near the water's edge and weighted its corners with four rocks he had chosen for their squareness. Jennifer sat down beside him with her notebook already open. Theodore stood a few feet back, arms crossed, wearing the expression of a boy who had been promised this would take twenty minutes.

"Mr. Bekele said if I can explain it to the two of you, out loud, then I actually understand it," Tyson said. "Not the textbook. Just the explanation." His placement exam for the college program was in nine days, and ocean circulation was the section he had failed in June, partly because he had memorized the arrows and never asked what the arrows were for.

Jennifer leaned over the map. The North Atlantic was drawn in bands of blue and red, arrows threading between them like veins. "So where is it," she said.

Tyson traced a ribbon of warm water leaving the Gulf of Mexico, riding up the American coast, then swinging northeast across the whole ocean toward Ireland and Norway. "That's the Gulf Stream. It carries warm water north, and that's part of why northern Europe is milder than you'd expect at that latitude." He said it flat, testing the sentence the way you'd test ice. Jennifer nodded slowly. Theodore did not move.

"Two and a half metres per second," Theodore said, which surprised them both, because Theodore had been silent since the fence. "At its fastest. I looked it up last night after you texted. It's one of the fastest ocean currents there is." He paused, then added, with visible reluctance, "That's about walking speed. A whole ocean, walking."

"An ocean that walks," Jennifer said, writing it down. "That's actually good. That's the kind of thing I'd remember."

Tyson looked at Theodore, who had spent all of junior year insisting that anything you couldn't measure was basically poetry, and that Tyson's interest in climate science was poetry with a spreadsheet attached. Now Theodore was standing at a flooded quarry on a Sunday, quoting current speeds. "You changed your mind," Tyson said.

"I got curious," Theodore said, as if confessing to something minor. "There's a difference."

Tyson tried again, and this time something happened that hadn't happened at his desk, or in the library, or during any of the spartan study sessions he'd imposed on himself since June, alone at the kitchen table with the phone in another room. He'd been thinking of the current as a fact to memorize, a thing to recite. But Theodore walked everywhere, everyone walked everywhere, and so he tried holding the map the way Theodore held the world, as quantities in motion. Two and a half metres per second, all the way across an ocean, warm water walking from the Gulf toward Norway, giving up its heat to the wind along the way, and the wind carrying that heat over Europe. That was the part people forgot, he realized, saying it out loud to Jennifer while she took notes: the current warms the air, and the air does the warming inland. The ocean was the engine, the wind was the delivery. Two systems, one effect. "You have to hold both at once," he said, "or you get the answer half right."

Jennifer stopped writing. "Say the last part again." He did. She wrote it, then read it back to him, and it held.

Mr. Bekele found them there an hour later, on his Sunday walk with his dog, as Tyson had half hoped he would. He listened while Tyson explained the whole thing twice, once plainly and once with the walking-speed comparison, and then he asked one question: how much of Europe's mildness comes from the current, and how much from other causes? Tyson opened his mouth, closed it. "I don't know," he said. "The map doesn't say. I'd have to look it up."

Mr. Bekele smiled at the water. "That answer will do fine on the exam," he said. "Better than a confident wrong one." He whistled for the dog and walked on along the fence line.

They stayed until the light went orange on the quarry walls. Theodore skimmed a flat stone across the grey water and it jumped four times before sinking. "So somewhere out there," he said, gesturing at nothing, at the whole ocean beyond the trees, "it's walking right now. Two and a half metres per second." Tyson folded the map along its old creases, and Jennifer, still writing, asked him to say the Ireland part one more time.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
The community hall smelled of lukewarm coffee and cardboard, and Olivia set the practice table three times before Mr. Adeyemi looked up from his clipboard. "Again," he said. "Candlesticks here, wine there, salt water where it can't be knocked over. You're hosting twenty people on Thursday, and your cousin's toddler will grab everything below knee height."

Olivia had volunteered for this in September, when her grandmother's hands had begun shaking too badly to hold the knife for the roast. Her mother had said, casually, that someone would have to lead the Seder this year, and Olivia had heard herself say her own name before she had finished deciding. Since then she had come to the hall every Tuesday with Mr. Adeyemi, the old man from the synagogue who ran the holiday prep classes, and she had learned the order of the plate, the timing of the readings, the way to pour without spilling. What she had not learned was what to do when her little brother covered his face.

His name was not on tonight's list, but he was there anyway, slumped in a folding chair with the practice Haggadah flat on his knees. He was nine, and in two weeks his class picture would show a boy with a black eye from the sidewalk, though right now he was only a boy who had been told, at Sunday supper, that this year the asking would fall to him.

"Say the first line," Olivia said.

"I know it."

"Then say it."

He pressed the book harder against his legs. "Why is this night," he began, and stopped as though the words had snagged on something in his throat.

Mr. Adeyemi had explained the structure back in March, but not the way a lecturer would; he had simply handed her the sheet. At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Olivia had read it once, looked at her brother, who was then eight and could barely read aloud in class, and thought nothing of it. Now it was the whole evening. The Seder could not move forward until someone asked why this night was different, and tradition said that someone was the youngest, and the youngest was hiding behind a paperback.

"It's just us here," she said. "Jessie and Iman already went home."

"Everyone will look at me."

"Everyone looks at everyone at the Seder. It's a room full of aunts. They look at you when you breathe."

He almost smiled. Then he closed the book entirely, which was worse.

Jessie had come to the first few sessions, joking that she wanted to know what she was getting herself into as Olivia's plus-one on Thursday. Iman had come once, sat through the geography of the Seder plate, and asked Mr. Adeyemi whether the youngest had to be a boy or could be a girl. Mr. Adeyemi had said tradition only said youngest, and Olivia had felt something turn over quietly in her chest, a possibility she had not let herself examine. She had pushed it away. It was her brother's job. It had been hers once, briefly, when she was small, before her cousins moved closer and a boy even younger arrived to take the role; she remembered standing on a chair at four, her grandmother whispering the first line into her ear, the whole table waiting. She remembered wanting very badly to be the one asking, and being told she had been, once, and now it was someone else's turn.

At the hall that night, she tried again. "Start from 'why.' Just 'why.'"

"Why."

"Good. Keep going."

"Is this night different," he said, and then his voice cracked and he said, "You do it. You're leading anyway. Nobody would know."

"People would know."

"They wouldn't. You can say you're doing it because Grandma can't. They'd believe that."

He was right, and she hated that he was right. If she asked the questions herself, she would be the youngest asking, which she was, if youngest meant what it had meant at Sunday supper, where her father had said her brother would be asking this year and no one had corrected him. She could stand up on Thursday, begin the Four Questions, and every adult at the table would impute the choice to necessity, to her grandmother's absence, to the general chaos of a family that had never had to think about it before. Nobody would say the word youngest. Nobody would have to.

She turned the idea over for a long moment, and it did not settle. One voice in her said the tradition was the point, the whole Seder was a machine built to make children speak; another voice said the tradition only required that someone able to do so ask, and her brother was not able, not this year, and a ritual that required forcing a terrified nine-year-old had lost something of itself. She could not fully reconcile the two. What she knew was that she was not impervious to the way his shoulders had climbed toward his ears, and that no one else in the family would notice, because at a table of twenty the loud children get the attention.

So she made him a deal, right there among the stacked chairs and the smell of old carpets.

"You ask the first question," she said. "One. Just the first one. When you finish it, I'll take the other three, and I'll stand up next to you so everyone's looking at me anyway."

He looked at the book. "That's not how it goes."

"How it goes is someone asks. Mr. Adeyemi said the youngest asks the questions; he never said they had to come out of the youngest all in one breath."

On Thursday, the candles were lit and the wine poured and the moment arrived, and her brother stood, and his voice shook, and he said, "Why is this night different from all other nights?" and sat down so fast he knocked over nothing at all, because Olivia had moved the salt water that morning to the far side of the table.
