Then she stood, one hand still on the back of his chair, and said, "Because on all other nights we eat leavened bread and unleavened, but on this night only unleavened," and in the pause before her aunt's question reached her, she felt her grandmother's eyes across the table, steady and bright, and heard her mouth the next line along with her, just as she had once whispered it into a four-year-old's ear.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, and people who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined.
story:
Charles set his fork down before he'd cut anything, because his mother had just asked, over the lamb, whether he'd decided. The polling place was the primary school two streets over, and tomorrow was Saturday, and he would be the only one at the table old enough to go.

"Mostly," he said.

"Mostly is not a vote," his father said, and reached for the water. His father had voted the same way his own father had, and mentioned this often, in the tone of a man describing the family recipe.

"Braydon says it doesn't matter because we're in a safe seat," Charles said. "Susan says that's exactly when it matters most, because margins get reported, and everyone reads them."

"Two friends, two theories," his grandmother said. She was staying the week, and she had taken the chair nearest the window so she could watch the street while she ate. "Which one do you like better?"

He liked parts of both, and it embarrassed him to say so, so he cut his lamb instead. Braydon's cynicism felt adult, almost sophisticated, and Susan's earnestness felt like something he was supposed to have grown out of but hadn't. Between them sat a whole way of being in the world, and tomorrow morning he was supposed to walk into a booth and pick one.

After dinner he took his plate to the kitchen, then his phone lit up on the counter with a message from Susan. He read it while the tap ran. She had been reading about other countries, she wrote, for a comparative politics thing, and she had found something that had knocked her sideways. Australia has used compulsory voting in federal elections since 1925, she typed. People who do not vote without a valid reason can be fined. She'd stared at that sentence for a full minute. Skipping a vote could cost you actual money, somewhere in the world. She didn't know whether she found that horrifying or beautiful, and she wanted to know which one he'd say it was.

He dried his hands and typed, then deleted it, then typed again. Her question was not really about Australia, and they both knew it. She was asking whether obligation made a choice worthless or made it real. He thought of Braydon, who called anyone who agreed with the popular kids a sycophant, rolling his eyes at compulsory anything, and he thought of his father voting a dead man's ballot out of loyalty, and neither of those felt like freedom to him either. The fine, he wrote finally, is like ten years overdue on a library book. It's not about the money. It's the country saying your absence is noticed. She sent back a single line, you notice me all the time, and then, before he could answer, I'm leaving early tomorrow, walk with me.

At breakfast his mother slid his enrolment card across the table without a word, which was its own kind of message, and his grandmother said the polling place would smell like floor cleaner and old glue, the way it always had. His father said nothing, but he had laid out two pieces of toast instead of one, and Charles understood this as an apology of sorts, an attempt to assuage whatever had hardened between them at dinner, and he took both pieces even though he wasn't hungry.

Outside, Susan was waiting at the corner with her own card in her back pocket, and the virulent posters on the telegraph pole behind her had been pasted over each other so many times that no candidate's face was legible anymore, only teeth and slogans in layers. They walked without deciding who had decided to walk. She asked him if he still didn't know, and he said he knew, mostly, but that mostly was as close as he was going to get, and that he thought mostly was what most people had and nobody admitted.

"Compulsory," Susan said, as they turned onto the school street, "is one word for it."

Inside the hall, the line moved slowly, and an old man ahead of them held his how-to-vote card upside down, and the volunteers with the pale green sashes were polite to everyone, including the ones who swore at them. When Charles reached the table, the woman found his name, drew a line through it with a ruler, and pointed him toward a screen. Behind it he stood for a moment with the pencil they gave you, small and stubby, half a dozen senators ranked below the house of representatives, the numbers waiting in the little boxes. He numbered the first one, then paused at the second, Susan's voice and Braydon's voice and his father's silence all crowded together, and then he kept going, one through six, in an order that was his, and that he would defend to some people and not to others.

He posted the ballot and stepped out into the sausage-sizzle smoke, where Susan stood holding two folded sheets she'd written something on the backs of, waiting for him to see.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Readers usually detect an unreliable narrator through contradictions, such as other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims.
story:
The book club met on Thursdays in the back room of the library, and Mr. Khoury had given them until the end of the meeting to decide who would present the novel at the school's reading festival on Saturday. Liam put his hand up before he could think better of it, mostly because Clement had elbowed him, and afterward he sat with the book open on his knee wondering what he had actually agreed to argue.

The novel was narrated by a man named Ellison who claimed, in the first chapter, that everyone in his village had loved him. The problem was that Liam had read the book twice and did not believe a word of it, and he could not yet say why in a way that would fill eight minutes at a podium.

"Try this," Lyra said, sliding her copy across the table. She had marked the margins with a green pen. "Every time somebody else in the book says something that doesn't match what Ellison says, I put a tick. I got to chapter four and ran out of margins."

Liam flipped through her pages. On page nine Ellison claimed his brother had begged him to stay. On page twelve the brother told a neighbour, in a letter Ellison himself was quoting, that he had changed the locks. On page thirty Ellison said the shopkeeper greeted him like a son; two pages later the shopkeeper charged him double and called him a liar in front of the queue. Every tick in Lyra's margins sat next to someone else's words, or next to an event, that contradicted something Ellison had claimed.

"So readers spot it like this," Lyra said. "Contradictions. Other characters' words, or the events themselves, don't match what the narrator claims." She said it plainly, the way she reported everything, and went back to her tea.

Mr. Khoury, shelving returns at the far wall, raised his head. "That's a defensible reading. Can you defend it, Liam? Saturday, mind. Eleven o'clock, the festival doesn't wait."

Liam started a list on the back of his festival registration form. He worked through the book a third time, chapter by chapter, logging every contradiction into a column. By chapter eight a pattern had hardened: the contradictions clustered wherever Ellison described himself as generous. Whenever money appeared in the plot, the other characters' accounts peeled away from his, and the events themselves went the other direction too, the loan he said he had forgiven showing up later as a debt collected with interest.

"You look like a geologist," Clement said, watching him. "Like you've found some stratum and you're brushing at it."

"Sort of," Liam said. "It's all one layer. Every lie is about the same thing."

Clement leaned over the list. "But here's my problem with your whole talk. Chapter fifteen. The flood. Ellison says he carried the widow's furniture out on his own back, and nobody contradicts him. Not her, not the neighbours, not the narrator's own events. So is he reliable there, or did the author just get tired?"

This was the part Liam turned over on the walk home, and turned over again while he made himself dinner and burned the rice. He had two ways of thinking sitting side by side in his head. The first said: the pattern holds, so the uncontradicted chapter is probably a lie the author left unexposed on purpose, and readers are meant to doubt it anyway. The second said: maybe Ellison was telling the truth that once, because people are not consistent, and a narrator who lies about money may not lie about floods. He could not find anything in the book that settled it, and Mr. Khoury had told them at the start of the term that a good reader says what stays uncertain instead of papering over it.

At the next morning's rehearsal, held in the empty drama room because the library was closed, Liam laid both readings side by side and admitted the gap between them. "I can prove he lies wherever money is involved," he said, tapping the list. "I can't prove anything about chapter fifteen. It might be the one true thing he says. That might be the point." His mouth had gone dry, the air in the drama room seeming to desiccate every word before it left him, and his voice came out thinner than he wanted.

Mr. Khoury, sitting in the back row with his coat still on, was quiet for a moment. "Keep that in," he said. "The uncertainty, I mean. Audiences trust a speaker who shows the seams."

A Year Eight class had booked the slot after his, and their teacher arrived early, querulous about the delay, gathering her students toward the door while Liam was still packing his notes. He had three minutes to decide whether to cut the chapter fifteen section for time or leave it whole, and Clement was holding the door, and Lyra was already halfway down the corridor with the timing stopwatch. Liam squared the pages, kept them all, and ran.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958; the resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.
story:
Hailey spread the printed graph across the picnic table and weighted its corners with river stones from the bucket by the fence, because the wind in her backyard had opinions about paper. The graph showed a line climbing in a jagged sawtooth, rising and rising, and beside it her notes said only: where does this come from? Ms. Becker had assigned the presentation on greenhouse gases for Friday, and Hailey understood the part about heat trapped by gases in the atmosphere, roughly, the way she understood that her grandmother's stove worked, which is to say not yet well enough to explain it to anyone else.

Darius arrived first, carrying two glass jars and a roll of plastic wrap, Maddox behind him with a thermometer borrowed from the chemistry room and a look of someone who expected to be blamed later. "So we're doing the jar thing," Darius said, setting them on the table. "One jar plain, one jar with carbon dioxide, both in the sun, see which gets hotter." Hailey said that was the plan, though she privately wondered whether a backyard could really stand in for an entire atmosphere, and whether the world allowed itself to be shrunk like that, folded into a jam jar on a July afternoon.

They taped the thermometer inside each jar, breathed into the second one through a straw until Darius declared it sufficiently "gassed up," and sealed both with plastic wrap. Maddox wrote the starting temperatures on the back of his hand, which Hailey pointed out was a vestigial habit from middle school, since they all had phones now, and Maddox said his hand had never once died on him.

While the jars sat in the sun, they turned to the graph. "Here's my problem," Hailey said, tapping the climbing line. "Everybody shows this picture, every article, every documentary, and nobody says where it comes from. Like it fell out of the sky already drawn." Maddox suggested it came from satellites. Darius suggested NASA. Hailey scrolled through her phone, then through her notebook, then through the textbook's fine print, where she found a footnote so small it seemed designed to abrogate the reader's curiosity, a reference to "continuous measurements" with no station named, no beginning, no person. "A graph has to have a substrate," she said, mostly to herself. "Somebody had to stand somewhere and measure something, over and over, for years, or there's no line at all."

The jars had been in the sun for twenty minutes when she found it, on a page she'd skipped twice because the title looked boring. A scientist named Charles David Keeling, of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, had begun regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958, high on a volcano, above the noise of cities and forests, one instrument taking the air's measure again and again. And the graph that came out of all that patient measurement had a name. "It's called the Keeling Curve," she read aloud, and then said it again because the words felt good in her mouth, a curve that belonged to a person.

"That's since before my parents were born," Darius said, leaning over the table, squinting at the sawtooth. Hailey noticed the little teeth of the line then, the small annual rise and fall, and wondered aloud what made the planet breathe like that within its longer climb. She didn't know, and the book didn't say, and she wrote the question in the margin next to a question mark she left uncircled, un-answered, honest.

Maddox called them back to the jars. The carbon dioxide one read four degrees higher than the plain one, which was not nothing, though Hailey cautioned the boys against pretending their backyard was the whole world. "It's a demonstration," she said, recording the numbers. "It shows the principle. It doesn't prove the planet." Darius argued that demonstrating was proving, more or less; Maddox argued that nothing proved anything; Hailey held her pencil above the notebook and said the jars showed how the idea worked while the Keeling Curve showed that it was happening, and that a person could hold both of those in her head at once without either one collapsing.

The sun moved off the table and the wind picked up, lifting one corner of the graph until the river stone clamped it back down. Hailey looked from the jars to the curve to the margin where her question sat waiting, and then she picked up the phone and a jar in each hand and carried them both toward the shade, holding them level, careful not to spill what was inside.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
Amelia found the gown in its plastic sleeve on her bed, folded the way the rental company had folded it, creases already settling into the shoulders like the garment had opinions about how she would stand. Her mother had left it there with the cap perched on top, tassel coiled, and a sticky note that said "iron on low, maybe." Below the note, in smaller handwriting, as though reconsidered: "Or don't. It's one morning."

The problem was not the gown. The problem was that Amelia had written a short speech, two minutes if she read slowly, for the ceremony's student slot, and last night the school had emailed to say that the honorarium attached to being chosen, two hundred dollars and a plaque, would instead go to a general fund, and that the speech itself was being trimmed to ninety seconds to keep the program on schedule. Ninety seconds. She had spent three weeks on it. Her father, when she read him the email, had excoriated the principal with a fluency she usually found funny and tonight found only loud, and her mother had said, from the kitchen, "It's still an honor, Mila," which was true and also, Amelia thought, tautological, since the honor and the speech were the same thing and saying so settled nothing.

She was still holding the printed pages at eleven the next morning when Paolo came over, carrying a bag of clementines because he believed all emotional crises had a citrus component. He let her read the whole speech aloud in the living room, standing, the way she would deliver it, and he ate two clementines and peeled a third he didn't want, which was his version of applause.

"You could just talk fast," he said.

"They'd cut the mic. Mr. Teo told me last year they cut a kid's mic because he went forty seconds over."

"Mr. Teo tells stories like other people tell weather."

Felix-Antoine arrived at noon, still in his work shirt from the garden center, smelling faintly of fertilizer and having thought about it, which was his way. He sat on the arm of the couch and asked what the speech was actually about, and when she said it was about endings, about how you spend four years learning a building and then they hand you a robe and walk you out of it, he looked at her with the mild, terrible patience of someone about to be right.

"You know what commencement means," he said. "Beginning. That's why they call it that. Graduates begin a new status, like being a bachelor or a master."

Amelia said she had assumed it was one of those words that meant the opposite of what it sounded, like inflammable, and Felix-Antoine said no, it was exactly what it sounded, and that she, specifically she, had written an entire elegy for a word that meant starting. Paolo laughed into his clementine. Amelia did not laugh, but she picked up the pages and read the first paragraph again, and the paragraph had changed shape without moving, the way furniture does when you finally look at it in daylight.

She spent the afternoon at the kitchen table cutting. It was not that her sadness had been wrong; she could hold both ideas, and she told them so over sandwiches, that the building would stop being hers and that the ceremony named for beginnings had mis-scheduled its own grief, and Paolo said that was the most Amelia sentence he had ever heard, and she threw a crust at him. She kept one line about endings because it was the truest line she had, and she built ninety seconds around it instead of filling ninety seconds with it, which was, she admitted, a better use of the constraint. The honorarium question she left alone. Money for words was a knot she could pick at in September, from a dorm room, with more distance.

The morning of the ceremony she ironed the gown on low, or anyway she moved a warm iron across it while occasionally checking her phone, and her mother took a photograph in the front hallway that Amelia would later like more than she expected to. At the school, in the hallway outside the gymnasium, Mr. Teo was adjusting his own hood with the doomed dignity of a man fighting velvet, and she asked him whether the two-minute rule had ever really cost anyone the microphone. He said, "One kid, 2011, and he deserved it," and then, softer, "Ninety seconds is plenty if you mean it."

When her name was called she crossed the stage without tripping, which she had privately ranked as the second most important achievement of the day, and when she stood at the podium the gymnasium was warmer than she'd practiced for, the cap's elastic already pinching. She looked out once, found Paolo's family and Felix-Antoine's bright shirt, and began. "They call this a commencement," she said, "because it means beginning, a new status, bachelor or master, and I spent three weeks writing about endings anyway, because I think we're allowed to do both." Then she turned the page, and read the line she had kept.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll: 200 people out of a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of about plus or minus 7 points.
story:
The poll arrived in Ryder's inbox on a Tuesday, forwarded by Martin with the subject line "front page, obviously." Twelve hundred adults surveyed, and somewhere inside it a table breaking off the youngest stratum, voters aged eighteen to twenty-four, who favored the transit ballot question by a margin of eleven points. Ryder read it three times during fourth period while Mr. Gupta wrote confidence intervals on the board, and by the bell he had already drafted the headline in his head: Young Voters Break for Transit.

Martin wanted it that night. He texted from his kitchen, apparently, judging by the photo of his laptop balanced on a toaster: "we run it thursday. everyone else will cover the topline, we own the youth angle." His want was simple and not subtle. The school paper had been dying politely for two years, and Martin believed, maybe correctly, that a story people under twenty-five would actually share was the only defibrillator left. Ryder sat at his desk with the poll open in one window and the half-written article in another, and did what he always did when a number looked too good: he checked it against the whole sample. The topline lead was seven points. The youth number was eleven. Both came from the same poll, the same plus or minus 3 margin of error stamped on the front page like a seal of freshness.

Here was the problem, and it took him most of Wednesday to see it. He was in Mr. Gupta's classroom after school, collating the poll's methodology tables with his own notes, when the shape of it surfaced. The fourteen hundred respondents in the whole poll carried that plus or minus 3. But the young-voters row rested on roughly two hundred people out of the thousand in the matched sample, and when he hunted through the appendix he found it in small print: a subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll. Two hundred out of a thousand carried about plus or minus 7 points. Eleven points of lead, minus seven in either direction, could be a landslide or could be nearly nothing. The headline in his head quietly dismantled itself.

"Subgroups," Jaidyn said the next morning, when he showed her the appendix. She was eating a granola bar in the back of the math classroom before first bell, feet on the rung of her chair. "That's the word, right? Larger margin of error than the whole poll. Plus or minus seven for your two hundred." She said it the way she said most things, flat and incisive at once, a knife laid on the table rather than swung. "So what are you going to do, bury the best number we've ever had?"

That was Jaidyn's want, and she owned it without embarrassment. She'd written three stories that year that no one read, careful stories about school board budgets, and she was tired of being right and unread. She thought precision was a luxury the paper couldn't afford anymore. "It's not lying," she said. "Eleven points is eleven points. It's in the poll."

"It's in the poll wearing a costume," Ryder said. "Seven either way. The topline's three. If I put eleven in forty-point font I'm telling people it means something it doesn't."

They took it to Mr. Gupta at lunch, not to be taught but to be referee. He listened with his arms folded, looked at the two margins side by side on Ryder's notebook, and asked exactly one question: "Which number can you defend if a reader calls you on it?" Then he went back to his sandwich, which was its own kind of answer, and left them standing there with the fact still between them.

Martin's reply, when Ryder texted him the appendix page, came as a voice message, and it was the most honest thing Martin had produced all week: a long exhale, then, "Fine. Fine. But write it so it's still a story. Make the uncertainty the story. 'Young voters lean transit, but the poll can't say how hard.' People like that, right? People like being told the truth gently?" He didn't sound convinced. He sounded like a person learning that defibrillators and honesty sometimes came in the same box.

Ryder wrote it Thursday morning in the empty math classroom, third period free, the poll open beside him. He kept the eleven, kept the seven, kept the three, gave the whole sample first and the subgroup after, and let the reader feel the floor flex under the number. When he got to the last line he sat for a while before typing it, because he still didn't know whether Jaidyn was wrong or just braver than he was, and the article didn't resolve that and neither did he. Then he hit send, and the draft went to Martin, who read it standing in the hallway outside the print lab, thumb moving slowly down the screen.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a).
story:
Kyle had told everyone, including himself, that he understood integration perfectly, which was the first thing that turned out not to be true. He had said it to Christine at lunch on Tuesday, and again to Mr. Siddiqui after class, and both times the statement had felt solid in his mouth, the way a thing does when you have repeated it enough. The exam was Saturday morning. The community centre on Fairfield Road ran a free tutoring room on Thursday nights, four long tables under fluorescent panels, and that was where Kyle planned to prove what he had been claiming.

The room smelled of floor wax and instant coffee. Mr. Siddiqui, who volunteered there on Thursdays and had apparently taught math for thirty years before retiring, set a worksheet in front of Kyle and said, "Show me where you are." Kyle looked at the first problem, the integral of x squared from zero to three, and reached for the method he trusted: rectangles. He drew the curve, sliced the region beneath it into strips, and began computing the area of each one. After the fourth rectangle he was still at the top of the page. After the eleventh he had drifted onto the margins, and the answers were only approaching the true area, never landing on it, like a bird circling a rooftop it could not quite settle on.

"You'll be there past midnight," said Karen, who sat across the table with her own sheet and, apparently, no faith in him at all. "And it still won't be exact."

"It will if I use enough rectangles," Kyle said, though he had begun to suspect, in the quiet way one suspects a friend of lying, that no number of rectangles would ever be enough. There would always be another slice to shave off or add on. He worked through a few more anyway, out of stubbornness, and the partial totals crept toward something like nine without ever saying nine.

It was Christine who tipped him over. She leaned across the aisle, pointed at a line in her notes, and said, "Look, there's a shortcut. If you find an antiderivative first." An antiderivative, her notes showed, was just the function you differentiated to get the one you started with. For x squared she had written x cubed over three. Kyle stared at that small, ordinary expression while the fluorescent light hummed above him, and a suspicion formed that he was almost afraid to test: that the whole mountain of rectangles could be replaced by two subtractions. If F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. He said it under his breath, once, to hear whether it held together. F of three was nine. F of zero was zero. Nine minus zero was nine, and nine was exactly where his rectangles had been circling all evening.

He checked it against the second problem, then the third, and each time the subtraction gave a number the rectangle sums had only approached. He felt a kind of exhilaration that he tried to keep off his face, because Karen was watching, and because he suspected that showing delight would admit how little he had actually known on Tuesday. Instead he imputed the discovery to the worksheet, as though the paper had arranged it, and told Mr. Siddiqui, "The sheet pretty much hands you the answer if you go backwards."

Mr. Siddiqui looked at him over his glasses. "The sheet handed you nothing. You found it because you spent forty minutes finding out why the rectangles couldn't finish." He let that sit, then moved on to the next table, where a voluble man from the evening ESL class was telling someone, at length, about the best way to fold samosas.

That was the part Kyle turned over on the walk home, hands in his pockets, past the lit windows of the laundromat. He had told people he understood integration, and he had not, and the difference between those two states had been invisible to him until Thursday night. But the method he trusted, the rectangles, was not exactly wrong either. It was the slow, honest road to the same place, the one that showed you what area actually meant, strip by strip. The shortcut was true, and the long way was true, and he could not decide whether the shortcut was a betrayal of the long way or its reward. He walked a block holding both of those positions at once, like a man carrying two bags and refusing to set either down.

On Friday he met Christine at the community centre again, in the same room, though the tutor tables were folded away for a seniors' card night. They took the bench by the window instead. He worked the practice exam straight through, using antiderivatives, quick and clean, and at the last problem he stopped and, out of some impulse he didn't examine, drew the curve and shaded the region beneath it. Then he checked his subtraction against the shaded shape, just to see them agree.

"Saturday, eight in the morning," Christine said, closing her binder. "Don't be late."

"I won't," said Kyle, and he looked once more at the shaded curve on his page before he turned it over.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
The community center kept its pianos in a room behind the gymnasium, two uprights pushed against a wall of mirrored tiles, and Autumn had the room from four to five on Thursdays because the ballet class had moved to Saturdays. She set her phone on the piano lid and opened the book Ms. Banerjee had left for her, folded open to a page marked with a receipt from the pharmacy. The piece was a Chopin waltz, and the eighth-note runs in the right hand kept collapsing whenever she reached tempo.

Kale came in at ten past four, carrying a duffel and a paper cup of coffee he wasn't supposed to have in here. He sat on the folding chair by the door and took out his history notes. "Don't mind me," he said. "The library's full of the debate kids and they're all yelling about metonymy. One of them keeps calling the White House the president and the other one keeps saying that's not how it works."

"It is how it works," Autumn said, not looking up. "The place standing in for the institution. We did it in English." She put her hands back on the keys and played the run again, and again it scattered, her fourth finger landing a half-beat late, the whole figure smearing like wet ink.

She stopped and dug through the bench. Under a stack of photocopied exercises was the metronome, a black plastic wedge with a dial on its face. She had never used it. Ms. Banerjee had mentioned it once, in passing, the way adults mention things they expect you to figure out. Autumn turned the dial and a light began to flash at the top, slow and patient. The markings on the face went up in increments, and the dial was set at 60.

"Is that thing broken?" Kale asked. "It's barely going."

"It's set to sixty," Autumn said. "Sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second."

She tried the run at that speed and it felt absurd, each note hanging in the air long enough for her to lift her finger, check it, place the next one. But the notes were right. All of them, every time, and after a few passes her fourth finger stopped arriving late because it had time to arrive at all. She played the figure ten times through, then twenty, and the slowness stopped feeling like punishment and started feeling like information. She could hear which intervals her hand wanted to rush.

The door opened and Felicia leaned in, gym bag on her shoulder, hair still damp from the pool. "I thought you quit," she said.

"I didn't quit. I was taking a break."

"That's not the same thing according to you, like, two weeks ago. You said either you commit or you don't."

Autumn kept her hands on the keys. She had said that, in the parking lot, the day she'd come home from school and found her mother had cancelled the lessons she'd paid for through June, on the grounds that the practicing was deleterious to Autumn's grades. Her mother had used a word like that, actually, had said it was "having a deleterious effect," as though the practicing were a medication with a listed side effect. Autumn had argued that a commitment was a commitment, that you couldn't just abrogate an agreement because it had become inconvenient, and her mother had said, "I'm the parent, I can abrogate whatever I want," which had ended the conversation.

"I changed my mind," Autumn said now. "You can slow down without quitting. It's still the same piece."

Felicia dropped her bag and came over to the piano. "Play it, then."

Autumn set the dial back to 60 and played the run at its crawling, exact pace, one note per beat where two belonged, then doubled it, two notes to each flash, and the figure held together for the first time. Not fast. Not the way it would eventually sound. But whole, every finger in order, and she could feel the shape of it in her hand the way you feel the shape of a sentence once you've finally said it correctly.

"See, you're good at this," Felicia said.

"I don't know if I'm good. I know I got it right once." Autumn moved the dial up one increment, and the light at the top began to flash faster. She laid her hands on the keys.

"Watch," she said.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
The line outside the community hall moved in short shuffles, and Nathan kept his voter registration card pressed flat against his thigh like something he might drop. He had turned eighteen eleven days ago, which meant the card had arrived before the birthday card from his grandmother, and he had not decided whether that said something about the country or about his grandmother. Behind him, Clementine was reading a sample ballot aloud in a flat voice, mocking the language of one of the questions, something about authorizing a bond issue, and every sentence of it was turgid beyond belief, swollen with clauses that seemed designed to make a person feel stupid for asking.

"It's like they don't want you to understand it," she said.

"Maybe that's the point," said Jase, who had come along even though he wouldn't be eighteen until March and could only stand outside the line, hands in his pockets, radiating the particular boredom of someone excluded from something he claimed not to want. "You're picking between two guys who'd both subjugate you the second they got the chance. Why does your one vote matter? It doesn't. Statistically it's nothing."

Nathan hated when Jase did this, mostly because the argument was hard to answer and partly because Nathan wasn't sure it was wrong. He had spent two evenings reading about the candidates and had ended up liking neither of them; one had the oily confidence of a born demagogue, the sort of man who could make a room feel agreed with, and the other had a record that read like a list of favors traded. The line moved again. Inside the hall, folding tables had been arranged under banners from the fall craft fair, and Mr. Mansour, who had taught Nathan's civics class two years ago and now apparently checked names against the ledger, was waving people forward with the weary efficiency of a man who had done this many times.

At the door stood Nathan's grandfather, holding a clipboard for the county party, and Nathan had the strange experience of seeing him as a fixture of the place rather than as a kitchen table. His grandfather had not said much on the drive over, only that he'd voted in every election since he was Nathan's age, and Nathan had not asked the question he'd been carrying around, because it felt like it would come out either rude or childish.

Jase answered it anyway, calling from outside the rope. "Hey, Mr. Kowalski. Tell Nathan why his vote matters, since you're the expert."

His grandfather looked at Jase for a moment, then at Nathan, and did not laugh. "You know how I got the vote at eighteen?" he said. "People my parents' age marched around saying old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Because eighteen-year-olds could be drafted and sent to Vietnam." He said it plainly, without the rise of a lecture, and turned back to his clipboard as if he had only reported the weather.

Nathan stood in the little booth with the ballot in front of him and found that the fact had changed the shape of the question. He was not deciding whether his vote mattered in the way Jase meant, whether one ballot could tip a total, because that had never been the claim; the claim had been about who counted as a person the country had to answer to. Men his exact age had been considered old enough to die for a decision and had been denied any say in who made it, and the vote had been moved to eighteen not because someone did the arithmetic on influence but because that contradiction had become unbearable to look at. He still didn't know whether his ballot was powerful. He knew it was his in a way that the draft card would have been his, and he noticed, filling in the first oval, that this made the act feel less like a choice between two men and more like refusing to hand the decision entirely to people who were not him. Which was not the same as hope. It might not even be the same as optimism. It was nearer to a door he could now walk through, whether or not the room behind it was worth entering.

He voted, then stood in the hall holding his "I Voted" sticker, waiting for Clementine, who was still squinting at the bond question with the ballot pen hovering. Jase had drifted inside and was reading the posted list of election officials, muttering that half of them were probably somebody's uncle.

"There's a write-in line," Clementine called to him. "Can I write in a name? Anyone?"

"It has to be a real person," Mr. Mansour said without looking up. "It can be a bad person, but it has to be a real one."

Nathan laughed, and his grandfather, still by the door, looked over and held out his hand, palm up. Nathan pressed the sticker into it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
story:
The folding chairs had been arranged on the football field in rows so straight they looked ruled, and William stood at the mouth of the corridor between the gym doors and the sunlight, wearing a gown that smelled like dry cleaning and someone else's graduation. The boy behind him, a tuba player named Kole, was humming the processional under his breath, the way people hum things they have known so long they have stopped wondering about them.

"That song," William said. "Where does it even come from?"

Kole kept humming for two more bars, then stopped. "No idea. It's just always been the graduation song. Like folding chairs."

William's phone was in his hand before he decided to take it out, and he typed the melody's name into the search bar even though he only knew it as la la la, dun, dun. The results loaded slowly on the crowded network. He had wanted one thing all morning, which was to walk across the stage before his father left for the parking lot, the way his father sometimes left from things, quietly, before they were finished. That want sat in his chest like a stone. But the phone loaded anyway.

Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, by Edward Elgar. It had premiered in 1901, in Liverpool. He read it twice. Liverpool, 1901. The tune that every graduate in North America shuffled to had been born in an industrial English port more than a century ago, for an audience of people who had never seen a folding chair on a football field. Nobody had invented it for graduations. It had just drifted here and stuck.

"Huh," William said, and held the screen out to Kole.

Kole read it, whistled low. "So it's not even ours. It's an import." He seemed pleased about this, the way he was pleased by most facts that made the ordinary world look slightly accidental. "That means some principal somewhere heard it and thought, yes, that's the sound of a diploma."

The line began to move. The gym doors banged open and the sunlight hit them all at once, and the band, seated near the concession stand, picked up the march with the particular slowness of student musicians who have been told to drag the tempo. William walked. He thought about his father, who had wanted him to take the business courses, and about Mr. Sandhu, who had wanted him to take the sciences, and about how nobody had actually asked him what he wanted, and how he had never exactly answered even when someone did. He had spent a year collating their opinions like a clerk with two stacks of paper, believing that if he stacked them neatly enough the right answer would emerge from the comparison. It had not. The confounder, he was beginning to see, was that both of them might be right, or neither, and that a choice could still be a choice even when it stayed partly blind.

Halfway down the corridor he understood something small and sharp: the march wasn't a graduation song at all, it was a borrowed thing that had become one, the way a borrowed opinion could become a conviction if you carried it long enough. He did not know yet whether that was a warning or a comfort. The ceremony went on around him, speeches, a tassel, someone's aunt standing on a cooler, and his name was called and he crossed the stage and shook hands and looked for his father's face in the bleachers and found it, still there, sunglasses on, which was something.

Kole had not expected to feel anything, and this annoyed him. He had come to graduation the way he came to most things, as an audience member of his own life, and now here he was in the third row feeling something shift in his chest every time the band stumbled back into that march. He watched William return to his seat with the diploma tube in his hand, holding it not like a trophy and not like a burden but like something he was still inspecting. Kole had known William since seventh grade, had watched him spend four years trying to be the sum of what other people wanted, and had privately considered this a capricious way to live, blown around by whoever spoke last. But the boy walking back down the row looked less blown than before, and Kole couldn't tell whether that was real or whether he was just sentimental today because of the horns.

He leaned forward and tapped William's shoulder. "So Elgar wrote a march for Liverpool in 1901, and now it's ours. What do you figure that makes us?"

William turned around, his cap slightly crooked. "Borrowers, I think. Everybody's a borrower." He said it without heaviness, and then, because the kid beside him had dropped her diploma tube and it was rolling, he stooped and caught it against his shoe and handed it back, and the band played on, slower than ever, and the line of graduates in the sun kept coming.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
story:
Connor set his fork down beside the rice because his mother had gone still, and stillness from her always came before news. Across the table his father was cutting chicken with unnecessary care, which meant he had known for hours.

"I got the letter from Aldersgate today," his mother said. "It came to the house."

Aldersgate was the scholarship foundation, the one that paid full tuition, and Connor had applied in October with an essay he now couldn't remember writing. He hadn't checked the mailbox in two days. He'd been avoiding it, though he would have called that superstition if anyone had asked, and he would have argued, if pressed, that he wasn't the kind of person who believed his not-looking could change what the envelope said. But he hadn't looked.

"The thin one or the thick one?" he asked.

"What?"

"Was the envelope thin or thick?" Everyone knew thick meant acceptance, packets and forms and welcome. Thin meant one page.

His father glanced up. "It's sealed on the counter. We didn't open it."

That was its own kind of mercy, or its own kind of test. Connor pushed back his chair, went to the counter, and carried the envelope back to the table, where he held it under the light as though thickness could be measured honestly that way. It felt thin. It felt like one page. He set it beside his plate and picked up his fork again.

"You should eat," his mother said, and then, softer, "Andres called twice while you were out."

Andres had a stake in all this too, though he'd never say it that way. He and Connor had applied to three of the same schools, and Andres needed the Aldersgate more, in the way that a person swimming needs the shore more than a person wading. His grades were a point lower, his father had been laid off in March, and he'd told Connor once, on the bleachers, that he was tired of teachers who pathologized every B, as though a transcript were a symptom. Piper had overheard and said, "You're not your GPA, obviously, but don't act like it doesn't count, either." That had started a two-day argument in the group chat that Connor had mostly watched from the margins.

He opened the envelope with a butter knife, slowly, the way you'd cut into something you suspected was still alive.

One page. But the first line said congratulations, and the second line said the award was conditional on final grades remaining consistent, and the third line, the one he read four times, said the foundation could not guarantee admission to any particular university, since the scholarship followed the recipient rather than creating one. He read it aloud because his mother's face was asking.

"So I got it," he said. "The money."

His father put down his fork. "But?"

"But the money isn't the admission." He was thinking of Piper now, of the argument he'd only watched. Piper had said grades were necessary, not sufficient, and Andres had said that was a coward's distinction, a way of pretending you knew something when you knew nothing. To prove it wasn't, Piper had used the sun. "The sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but it's not sufficient, because something may cast a shadow." A building, a cloud, your own hand. The sun could be up and you could still be standing in the dark.

"It's like that," Connor said. "The scholarship needs me to get in somewhere, but it doesn't get me in. I could have the money and no place to use it."

His mother reached over and turned the letter toward herself, though her eyes stayed on him. "So it's good news."

"It's necessary-good," he said. "Not sufficient-good."

His father laughed once, short, surprised out of himself. His mother did not laugh. She was already somewhere ahead of them, he could see it in her jaw, at the admissions offices, at the waitlists, and he understood that for her this letter was one door opening onto a corridor of further doors, some of which would be locked no matter what he carried.

He texted Andres from the hallway after dinner. Full ride, but conditional. Then, before he could stop himself: what did you get. The typing dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again. He stood in the hallway with the phone held in both hands, listening to his mother run water in the kitchen, watching the dots pulse like something deciding whether to surface.

"Call you in five," Andres wrote. "Don't tell Piper yet."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The portal refreshed to the same screen it had shown for eleven days: your application is complete, thank you for your patience. Jordan had come to know every pixel of that sentence. He pulled the laptop closer on the kitchen table, closed the tab, opened it again, and the sentence was still there, patient as ever, more patient than he was.

His mother put a glass of milk beside the keyboard without comment. She had agreed, after some negotiation, not to ask about the decision until the decision existed, and she honored the terms so strictly that the silence around the topic had become its own kind of pressure. He heard her sequester herself in the living room with the television on low, which was her way of staying near without hovering.

Rian arrived at four with his own laptop under his arm, on the theory that filling out applications side by side was less unbearable than filling them out alone. He set up across the table, plugged in, and started typing his activities list. "I'm doing the essay about my grandmother's garden," he said. "You still doing the one about the crosswalk?"

"The crosswalk," Jordan said. He had written four hundred words about standing at an intersection every morning, watching people decide, in half a second, whether to trust the drivers turning right. The essay had taken him two months. It was the only part of the application he was sure of.

Damon texted a screenshot of his own submitted confirmation and added, "done forever unless they say no." Then he called, because Damon could not send good news without also narrating it. "You know we only had to write this stuff once?" he said. "My cousin applied in like 2005 and she told me she had to fill out every school separately. But we used the Common Application, one form, all my schools. My dad looked it up. It was founded in 1975 with fifteen member colleges. Now it has more than a thousand."

"I know," Jordan said. "I'm on it right now."

"One essay, twelve schools," Damon said. "I would not have survived twelve separate essays. I would have enrolled at the gas station." He hung up, and Jordan sat with the phone in his hand for a moment, thinking about the strange economy of it, one version of yourself, written once, multiplied a thousand ways to a thousand committees. Whether that was mercy or flattening he could not decide, and the two ideas sat side by side without merging.

Rian leaned over. "Decision's not up?"

"December fifteenth," Jordan said. "Supposedly."

Rian went back to his essay. Jordan refreshed once more, and the page stuttered, and where the patient sentence had been there was a new line in blue: an update has been posted to your application. His hands went cold on the keys. It was eleven days early. He thought, with a clarity that felt borrowed from someone else, that he could simply close the laptop and walk to the park and never know, and that this option was available to him for exactly as long as he did not click.

He clicked. The update was not the decision. It was a request from the admissions office for his first-quarter grades, which the school had apparently failed to send, a single missing transcript from a single counselor's office, and it had been missing for eleven days while the portal told him his application was complete. He called the counselor's office and got a recording. He called the school's main line and got the putative receptionist, who transferred him to a voicemail that was full.

"Drive over there," Rian said.

"The office closes at four thirty."

"Then run."

Jordan ran. It was a mile and a half to school, past the crosswalk from his essay, where the light turned and nobody was waiting. The front doors were locked but the side entrance by the gym was still open, and he found the counselor, coat already on, locking her file cabinet. She listened, checked, and found the transcript in a folder on her desk, printed and stamped and somehow never scanned, a whole future delayed by a piece of paper that weighed nothing. "I'll send it tonight," she said. "First thing. I'm so sorry, Jordan."

He walked home in the dark, cooled down, the panic gone and something more complicated in its place. He had wanted the answer, and instead he had learned that the answer was being decided on an incomplete file, that the version of him sitting in that admissions office belonged to a genus of applicant he had never imagined, the file with a hole in it. He would never know what the committee would have concluded about the incomplete version. That uncertainty was permanent now, a branch of the tree that had been sawed off before anyone saw where it led.

At home his mother was still in the living room, television off now. Rian had left a note on the laptop: refreshed for you twice, still nothing, hang in there. Jordan sat down, opened the portal, and began composing an email to the admissions office, explaining the delay, attaching nothing yet, stating the facts in plain sentences, one by one, the way you state things when you cannot control what comes back. Behind him his mother came to stand at the doorway, and he heard her stop there, waiting, saying nothing, one hand on the frame.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Florida Straits and north along the east coast of the United States.
story:
Mr. Somsak had a habit of assigning things he refused to teach. "You'll present Friday," he said, dropping a laminated ocean current map on John's desk like a court summons. "Gulf Stream. Two minutes, no notes. Convince us Europe isn't freezing by accident." He walked away before John could lodge a complaint, which John took as a personal challenge and, later, as an act of mercy.

The problem was that John did not understand the map at all. It looked like a weather forecast drawn by someone having a breakdown, all looping arrows and temperature bands. He'd stared at it Thursday night until the arrows seemed to move on their own, which they technically did, but not for the reasons his tired brain suggested. His mother offered the opinion that oceans were big, which was true and useless, roughly the dimensions of his project so far.

"It's a museum, not a punishment," Madisyn said Friday morning, hauling him past the ticket counter by his sleeve. "Kallie works the ocean hall on Fridays. She says they have a current map the size of a garage door." John had planned to spend his free period hyperventilating quietly in the library, but Madisyn had a policy of not letting him do that, a policy she had never bothered to codify but enforced with the rigor of a customs officer. He didn't even want to think about what she'd charge him for this rescue. Some indemnity, surely, in snacks or a week of carrying her lab notebooks.

The map was, in fact, the size of a garage door, glowing on the wall of the dim ocean hall. Kallie found them standing in front of it like men before a shrine. "So you're the crisis," she said. "Madisyn texted me a whole paragraph of capital letters." She handed John a plastic pointer, then took it back, then handed him nothing at all. "No pointer. Trace it with your finger. You'll remember it better, and also it's funny watching you reach."

He started at the warm swirl of the Gulf of Mexico, because that was the only part of the map he recognized with any confidence. "Here," he said, and dragged his finger east and through the narrow gap between Florida and Cuba. "That's the Florida Straits, right? It squeezes through there." The channel was vivid on the map, a river of red and orange threading between landmasses. Then the color ran up along the coast, hugging the eastern seaboard, past the Carolinas, past where he guessed New Jersey was, a warm stripe pressed against the continent like a scarf against a neck. "It goes north. Up the whole east coast of the United States. Then it just... leaves. Swings out into the Atlantic."

"Congratulations," Kallie said, "you have discovered that water moves. There's a plaque and everything." But she said it while nodding at the northeastern edge of the map, where his finger was hovering over the smeared arrow that carried the warm colors off toward Europe. He followed it. It crossed the whole cold blue of the North Atlantic and ended, on the map's far margin, at the British Isles, at Norway, at places that by latitude should have been as bitter as Labrador but weren't. He put his palm flat over Britain and felt, under the laminate, only wall, and still something in him registered it as warmth, a visceral certainty that he was touching the reason Edinburgh had rain instead of permafrost.

"So the warm water comes out of the Gulf of Mexico," he said slowly, "through the Florida Straits, rides north along our coast, crosses the ocean, and hands its heat to Europe. The same current. One delivery." He turned to Madisyn. "That's the whole thing. That's my two minutes." She considered it. "You'll need to talk slower, you talk like a raccoon when you're nervous. And do the finger thing, the tracing. Mr. Somsak loves a finger thing."

Fifth period, John stood at the front with the classroom's sad projector version of the map, which was the size of a pizza box and blurred at the equator. He traced the route anyway, Gulf to straits to coast to ocean, narrating each leg, and when he finished, Mr. Somsak asked the question John had been dreading: "Why does the current cross instead of just staying along the coast?" John opened his mouth, then closed it. "I don't know yet," he said. "The map shows where, not why. I'm still working on why." A boy in the second row snickered, but Mr. Somsak wrote something in his binder and said nothing, and Kallie, who had materialized at the door with a hall pass of dubious provenance, gave him a thumbs up.

Afterward Madisyn caught up with him in the corridor. "You admitted you didn't know," she said. "In front of everyone. Bold." "Terrifying," John corrected. "It was terrifying." But he was already looking at his phone, thumbing through search results with the expression of a man who has just found out the world's largest library lives next door. "Tonight," he said, "I find out why."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
Coralie had watched the Under-12 girls lose the ball eleven times in the first half, and nine of those times the pass had died on the end of a defender's outstretched leg. She stood at the edge of the field with her clipboard, a sixteen-year-old handed a team for the first time because the real coach was away at a wedding, and she noticed something the parents shouting from the sidelines apparently had not: the girls were not passing badly. The passes were straight, reasonably weighted, aimed at feet. They just travelled along the ground, where every defender's leg in the world was waiting to meet them.

At halftime she gathered them by the bench, and they looked up at her with the frank, unimpressed faces of children who know an impostor when they see one. She wanted to fix everything at once, and she knew that was the impulse of someone who had never taught anything. So she made herself introspect for a moment, to look inward at what she actually wanted, and found it was smaller than glory: she wanted the next half to have one more completed pass than the last one.

That night she sat at her desk not with drills but with a memory. Two winters ago she had been at her neighbour Mr. Jung's place, snowed in until her mother could fetch her, and he had let her watch the third period of a game with him. A player had flicked the puck up, barely, so it rose just off the ice, sailed flat over an opponent's stick, and came down softly on his teammate's blade. Coralie had leaned forward and asked what that was, and Mr. Jung had said, around a mouthful of pretzels, "Saucer pass," and then nothing more, because he was a man who believed the game should explain itself. She had spent the rest of the period counting them, wondering why some landed perfectly on the blade and some bounced away, noticing that the flat ones in the air were the ones that arrived cleanly.

She turned this over now. The puck lifts just off the ice so it flies flat over the opponent's stick and lands right on the receiver's blade. That was the whole trick. Not height, not power. A little lift, a flat flight, a soft arrival. On a soccer field the geometry was the same in her mind's eye, only translated: a defender's leg instead of a stick, grass instead of ice, a teammate's foot instead of a blade. She wondered whether it would translate at all, really, or whether she was about to teach ten-year-olds something that only worked in her head.

The next morning she found Sarah-Maude in the caf, because Sarah-Maude played wing on the school team and had opinions about everything, and Kiefer, who was there only because Sarah-Maude was. Coralie laid out cones on the hallway floor, no ball, just the idea. "You know how your passes keep getting eaten by that team with the tall girl?" Sarah-Maude said the defenders' sticks, the legs, whatever you wanted to call them, were always low, always sweeping the ground. "So why does everyone pass along the ground?" Coralie asked. Nobody answered. Kiefer said the thing she kept thinking about afterward: "Maybe because ground passes are what everyone's taught first, so they're what everyone defends first." It sounded almost like something from her history class, the way historiography worked, where the records you inherit decide the story you can tell. The girls on her team had inherited the ground.

So she built a drill. Cones for defenders' legs, laid flat in pairs. A low stick actually, borrowed from the gym teacher's floor-hockey bin, held sideways by whoever's turn it was to be the villain. The rule was simple: the ball had to go over the stick and land inside a chalked box before the receiver's foot, one bounce or none. Not a lob, not a clearance. A small, flat, polite lift. The first girl to try it banged the ball high into the wind, and Coralie called it back with her whistle and asked her to try being lazier about it, which made the girl laugh, which was the first laugh of the morning.

By the third attempt someone did it, a girl named only on her shirt as number seven, the smallest one. The ball rose the width of a hand, floated over the stick almost diaphanous in the low sun, and dropped into the box, where number nine trapped it dead. The whole line went quiet, then noisy. "Again," Coralie said, and they went again, and again, and she crouched by the stick-holder with her clipboard, saying nothing, watching to learn what she could not plan: which kids lifted too much, which not at all, which ones understood in their feet before they understood in their heads.

Saturday the tall girl played. Coralie stood on the touchline with her heart in her throat and her clipboard untouched, because the game was not hers anymore. In the fourteenth minute, number seven received with her back to pressure, and Coralie saw her look up, saw the defender's leg slide across the grass exactly like the flat cones at practice, and then the ball left her foot and rose, just, so little that the defender flinched too late, flew flat over the leg and landed at number nine's feet, one bounce, into the net path, shot, saved. Saved, and the parents groaned, and number seven turned toward the sideline.

Coralie raised one fist anyway. She did not know yet whether one clever pass against one clever girl made a coaching philosophy, or whether she had taught them something true about soccer or only something true about one Saturday. She would find out the way she found everything this week, by watching. Number seven was still looking at her, breathing hard, grass on both knees. "Did you see it?" the girl shouted across the half-mown field, and Coralie pushed off the post and walked toward her whistle in hand.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key, so a movement in C major moves to G major.
story:
The organ loft of St. Brigid's smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Mr. Farah had let Alexandre use the folding table up there on the condition that he touch nothing with pipes attached to it. Alexandre spread the score of Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, across the table and weighted the curling pages with two hymnals and a tin of valve oil he had found and decided not to ask about. He had until Thursday to hand in an analysis: mark the exposition, the development, the recapitulation, and justify every bracket with a bar number.

Meliane came up the spiral stairs with her earbuds still in, one dangling, which was her way of arriving. She set down two coffees, expropriated the better one for herself on the principle, she said, that she had climbed more stairs than he had, and looked over his shoulder at the dense pencil marks already crowding the first system.

"You've written 'second theme?' four times," she said. "With question marks."

"Because I keep hearing it wrong." He tapped the page. "The first theme is obviously C major, it's practically a scale, that part's a gift. Then somewhere around here a new tune arrives, the lyrical one, and I keep thinking, there, that's the second theme. But when I check the key signature it hasn't changed yet, and Mr. Farah says the second theme in a major-key sonata usually shows up in the dominant key. C major's dominant is G major. So the new tune has to be in G, or it isn't the second theme, it's just a transition wearing a costume."

Meliane pulled out the loose earbud, wound it around her finger, unwound it. "So listen for the tune and then check the score for the key."

"That's the whole method, yes."

"Then why the four question marks?"

He didn't have a good answer, so he pressed play on the battered speaker and they both leaned in like people at a séance. The first theme went by, cheerful and dumb in the way only Mozart is allowed to be. Then the music began to slide, and Alexandre held his pencil over the score, not writing, hovering. At the moment the new tune arrived, warm and singing over a bubbling left hand, he stabbed the page. "There."

Meliane bent down, ran her finger along the key signature at the start of that line. "One sharp."

"G major," he said, and felt something settle that had been rattling around since Sunday. He drew the bracket, wrote the bar number, then sat back and looked at what he'd written, which was less than he'd expected to have by now.

The problem, and he said this out loud because Meliane was the kind of person you said things out loud to, was that his ears and his eyes were giving him two different stories. His ears wanted to call the second theme the moment anything lyrical happened, wherever it happened. His eyes wanted the key change, the one sharp, the rule. The rule was winning, obviously, because the rule was what Thursday's assignment would be graded against, but he wasn't sure the rule was the same thing as the truth. Maybe the tune started being the second theme before the key signature got around to admitting it. Maybe Mozart liked leaving the door half open. He marked the key change with a firm bracket and, in the margin, a small honest question mark, which he then crossed out, which he then crossed the crossing out of, leaving a small grey nest of graphite.

Mr. Farah climbed the stairs at six to lock the loft, moving with the unhurried economy of a man who had spent forty years ascending to an organ bench and had made an ascetic discipline of never hurrying the climb. He glanced at the score, at the bracket, at the marginal nest. "G major," he said, mildly, as if confirming the weather.

"Second theme," Alexandre said, trying to sound more certain than the pencil did.

Mr. Farah looked at the crossed-out question mark for a long moment. Then he picked up the tin of valve oil, pocketed it without comment, and went back down the stairs, his footsteps unhurried to the end. Meliane watched him go, then turned to Alexandre with an expression of studied, nonchalant innocence.

"So is the question mark staying or going?"

Alexandre looked at it, the small grey tangle, honest and inconvenient. He picked up the eraser, held it over the page, and set it back down.

"It's staying," he said, and drew the development bracket.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
Grace had claimed the computer by the window in the public library every Saturday since October, and the librarian, Mr. Santos, had stopped asking for her library card. She was working on her application to universities in the United Kingdom, which meant working through UCAS, the central admissions service, and the whole thing had a smell of finality she distrusted. On the screen was a page of instructions she had read four times without quite believing.

Her cousin Priya had gone through this three years ago and had sent Grace a long email about the personal statement: one free-form essay, four thousand characters, the story of your life angled toward your subject. Grace had drafted that essay twice. The first version was about metaphysics, which was what she wanted to study, and it was terrible, all fog. The second version opened with her grandfather's funeral, which was better but felt borrowed, as if grief were a currency the admissions office accepted. She had both drafts saved on a USB drive in her pocket.

"What are you staring at?" Alexzander dropped into the chair beside her with a geometry textbook he had no intention of opening. He was applying to schools in the state, early decision, and considered her British plan a form of self-punishment.

"The format changed," Grace said. "For people starting in 2026. It's not one big essay anymore." She scrolled so he could see. "Three structured questions instead. Why you want the subject, and how you've prepared for it."

"That's it? No life story?"

"That's it."

Alexzander leaned back. "Priya's going to feel old."

Francesco arrived at noon with two sandwiches and an opinion. He had read somewhere that structured questions were a trap, that they flattened everyone into the same three boxes, that the free-form statement had been the one place an applicant could be a person. He argued this while eating, so the argument came out in fragments, but Grace took it seriously, because Francesco's arguments were usually half right. She remembered Priya's email: the essay as performance, hours spent cutting a self down to four thousand characters. Maybe the boxes were a mercy. Or maybe they were a cage with nicer bars.

She opened a blank document and typed the first question at the top. Then she sat without typing for a while. The library fermented quietly around her, if a stillness could ferment: a man at the far table whispering into a phone, a child reshelving picture books in the wrong order, the radiator ticking. Grace thought about the difference between showing and proving. The old essay let you show. The new questions made you prove, and proving felt uglier, more like a courtroom, but it also felt harder to fake. She had been planning to write around the fact that she had never formally studied philosophy, that her preparation was a shelf of secondhand paperbacks and one wet October spent reading them on a bus. Under the old rules she could have dressed that up. Under the new rules she had to say it.

She typed: I have not taken a course in this subject. Then she kept going, listing what she had instead, and the list surprised her by being longer than she expected, though each item on it felt evanescent, the kind of thing that proved nothing to anyone who had not been there. She stopped trying to make the list sound like more than it was. She typed: I read them anyway.

"Is that a sentence or a confession?" Francesco asked, reading over her shoulder.

"Both," Grace said. She deleted the funeral opening from her mental draft entirely, then, for a moment, put it back, then took it out again. The truth was she could not decide which Grace the admissions tutors should meet, the one who argued with books on the bus or the one who could write four polished paragraphs about wanting to understand what exists. For the first time she considered that these might be the same person, and that the questions, by forcing the second to account for the first, were doing something the free-form essay had never required.

Mr. Santos passed with a cart of returns and paused at her screen. "Deadline soon?"

"January, for most of them." Grace saved the document. "But I want it done before winter break."

"Then you have time to be wrong twice," he said, and moved on.

She wrote until four, filling in the second question, the preparation one, with the paperbacks and the bus and a Tuesday when she had explained determinism to Alexzander until he threatened to leave. Francesco read it and said the paragraphs were still uneven, and Grace said she knew, and did not fix them evenly, because even was not what she was after anymore. Alexzander closed his geometry book unread and asked if she wanted a ride home.

"In a minute," she said. She read the last paragraph once more, changed a single word, and pressed save. Outside, the streetlights had come on. She slid the USB drive into her pocket, where it clicked against her keys.

"Ready?" Alexzander said from the doorway.

"Almost," Grace said, and logged off.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy.
story:
Anna had the paper tucked inside her chemistry folder, the Hebrew transliterated in her own handwriting, and she read it under her breath while the kettle heated. "Baruch atah Adonai," she whispered, and the words felt like a stranger's coat on her shoulders, warm but not hers. Her grandmother had flown in on Thursday, and tonight was the first night of the holiday, and for reasons nobody had explained, her father had said, "Anna, you'll do the Kiddush this year." Not her older brother. Her.

She had looked it up on her phone in the parking lot before driving home with her mother, scrolling while the car idled. Kiddush, the screen said, is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy. She read it three times, then practised under her breath the whole ride, the steering wheel steady under her mother's hand, the streetlights sliding across the windshield. Her mother said nothing, which Anna understood to mean something.

"You're going to be great," Matthieu had told her at school, when she'd confessed the assignment over cafeteria fries. "It's like a presentation. You do presentations." But it wasn't like a presentation, and she hadn't known how to say why. At a presentation nobody's grandmother was listening with her eyes closed. At a presentation you weren't standing where your grandfather had stood every year until last spring, when he quietly absconded from every duty of his old life and moved into the room with the hospital bed by the window, the room everyone in the house called "Grandpa's study" and then, after a while, stopped calling anything at all.

In the kitchen now, her grandmother was showing her how to fill the silver cup, the one with the dented rim that had survived three moves and one drop on a tile floor in 1998. "Not to the top," her grandmother said, turning the cup so the light caught it. "To here. A little less." Her hands were spotted and steady. Anna watched and thought, canny, the way she watches everything before she touches it, and then felt ashamed of the word, as if she'd caught herself appraising a queen.

"Why me?" Anna asked. She kept her voice light, aiming for curiosity rather than grievance, but the question landed heavier than she'd meant, the way questions in this kitchen always did.

Her grandmother set the cup down. "Your grandfather asked for you."

"But Danny's older. Danny knows more Hebrew than I do."

"Your grandfather," her grandmother said again, and began wiping a counter that was already clean.

Flashback: Anna at nine, sitting on the carpeted step of Grandpa's study while he recited the blessing, his voice dropping into a register she'd never heard him use anywhere else, scolding plumbers, arguing about baseball. She had asked him once what the words meant, and he'd said, "It means we're setting this night apart from the other nights," and she had thought he meant it like setting a table, arranging things, and only years later realized he might have meant apart, separate, holy in the way her mother meant it when she said certain things couldn't be joked about.
