The door opened and Danny came in with grocery bags, and Mila behind him, home from her first semester and loud about it. "Is that the cup?" Mila said, dropping bags on the table, nodding at the silver. "Anna, you're doing it? Since when?" And there it was, the subtext Anna had been circling all afternoon, arriving in Mila's bright, thoughtless voice: since when does the youngest granddaughter, the one whose Hebrew comes off a phone screen, take the grandfather's place?

"Since Dad asked her," their grandmother said, in the tone of a woman closing a door.

"Right," Mila said. "Obviously. No, it's cool. It's just, like, sudden." She started unpacking groceries too quickly, cans clacking into the cupboard, and Anna understood that Mila wasn't angry at her, or not only at her; she was angry at the year, at the room upstairs, at the fact that everything had changed without a vote.

Dinner came together in the kitchen's usual chaos, the table extended with the wobbly leaf, the candles lit by her mother, her grandmother muttering that the soup was too hot and not hot enough in the same breath. When the moment came, Anna lifted the cup and felt the whole room arrange itself around her, her father's hand on Danny's shoulder, Mila's phone face-down for once, and she began. She got the first line out clean. On the second she stumbled, stopped, and heard her own heartbeat, and her grandmother's voice came in beside her, quiet, carrying her over the broken place like a hand under an elbow. They finished the blessing together, half a beat apart, and the sound of it was imperfect and doubled and real.

Later, in the doorway of the study, the silver cup still in her hand, Anna stood where the light from the hallway fell across the bed. "I did it," she said. "I stumbled on the second line. Grandma had to help."

Her grandfather's eyes opened. "Everyone stumbles on the second line," he said. "Your grandmother carried me for forty years." He patted the blanket beside him, and she came and sat down, holding the cup so the dented rim caught the lamplight.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Haggadah is the book read aloud at a Passover Seder; it retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt.
story:
The synagogue library smelled of dust and old glue, and Ethan spread the photocopied pages across the table the way Mr. Santoso had shown him, spine side up so nothing cracked. Fourteen people at his grandmother's table on Monday night, and all of them would be looking at him. His father had led the Seder every year until this one, and his father had said, the way he said most things now, carefully and from a distance, that it was time.

"It's just a dinner," Ella had told him at school, watching him panic over a folded photocopy during study hall. "Your family eats, someone mumbles, everyone goes home."

"It's not just anything," Ethan had said, and then hadn't been able to explain why, which bothered him more than the panic did.

Mr. Santoso, who ran the library on Sundays and fixed the sanctuary's speakers when they hummed, found him there with the pages fanned out and the pencil chewed. "You're the one leading for the Feldmans," he said. It wasn't a question. He sat down anyway, uninvited, and turned one of the pages right side up. "So read me the part with the four children."

Ethan read it, his voice going thin on the long Hebrew. When he finished, Mr. Santoso said nothing for a while, and Ethan understood the silence was the point of him, that Mr. Santoso taught by making room.

"Here's what nobody tells you," Mr. Santoso said finally, tapping the stack of pages. "This is the Haggadah, the book read aloud at a Passover Seder. It retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt, start to finish, out loud, everyone taking a turn. So the leader's real job isn't reading. It's handing out the turns." He pushed the pages toward Ethan. "Fourteen people. Some of them read well. Some of them, your uncle, will turn every passage into a speech. Who's at the table?"

Ethan had never thought of it as a seating chart of egos. He started writing names in the margins, and Mr. Santoso corrected him gently, once, about a great-aunt who'd gone blind and would need the large-print pages, and then left him alone with the humming speakers and the work.

At home, his father looked over the marked-up pages and frowned. "You gave yourself the long sections," he said.

"They're the ones in the middle where nobody's paying attention anyway," Ethan said. "I gave the four questions to Mira. She's nine, and it's her first year old enough."

His father turned to the window. For a month Ethan had watched him decide whether his exhaustion was something to pathologize or just to endure, whether naming it would shrink it or hand it power, and neither of them had won that argument yet. "Your grandfather used to give the boring parts to the people he was punishing," his father said, almost smiling. "Don't do that."

Monday night, the table stretched into the living room with a folding card table at the end for the kids, and Ethan stood with his glass of juice while fourteen faces waited. He had practiced the blessings until Mahdi, who had come over to study for calculus and stayed for the practice run, could recite the order of them himself. Mahdi sat now at the far end, wedged between two cousins, watching Ethan with the flat attention of someone who knew exactly how nervous he was.

Ethan began. He stumbled once, on the second blessing, and kept going. When they reached the passage about the wise child, he handed the page to his uncle, who read it at half speed with a pause after every clause, and Ethan let him, because the man had flown in from Denver and this was his only part. When they reached the passage about the wicked child, one of the cousins snorted and muttered something about the whole thing being a revisionist fantasy anyway, and Ethan said, "You get the next one," and the cousin read the next one, and that was all that was said about it.

His grandmother caught his eye somewhere in the middle of the meal and raised her glass a little, a gesture so small that only he could have read it. She had told his father, in the kitchen, that Ethan was more sagacious at seventeen than his grandfather had been at fifty, which Ethan had overheard and did not believe, but he had carried the sentence around all evening anyway like a stone in his pocket.

He still didn't know if he believed the exodus happened the way the book said, or if that was even the question the book was asking. He handed his father the pages for the section on the plagues, ten drops of wine pressed out one at a time, and watched his father's finger find its place. Then Ethan poured the water into the red wine for Elijah's cup, both hands steady, and set it at the door.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, the narrator Holden Caulfield tells readers, 'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.'
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and orange peel, and Luke had the essay prompt folded into his pocket like a confession he hadn't committed yet. Ms. Mercado had written it on the board before the bell: whose version of events do we trust, and why. He'd copied it down without thinking, which was the problem. He never thought on buses. The bus was for watching the parking lot slide by and arguing with Adriano about nothing.

Today Adriano was arguing about something. "I don't get why we're supposed to care," he said, leaning over the aisle with his earbud half out. "The guy just talks for two hundred pages. Nothing happens. My dad says he read it in school and everyone thought Holden was deep, and now everyone thinks he's annoying."

"Both can be true," Luke said.

"That's not an answer."

Francesca, two rows up, turned around. She had the paperback on her knees, swollen with sticky tabs, which Luke found frankly aggressive. "You're on the part where he fights his roommate, right? Stradlater."

"Did you tab the whole thing?" Luke asked.

"I tabbed the lies."

That was the sentence that undid him, though he didn't know it yet. He took out the prompt and read it again. Whose version of events do we trust. It had seemed like a question for a different kind of student, the kind who used words like hermeneutics and owned a copy of the novel that hadn't been purchased at a gas station. But Francesca had tabbed the lies, which meant the lies were trackable, which meant they were a pattern and not a mood.

"Wait," Luke said, and got up and moved into her row before he'd decided to, which the driver registered with a long look in the mirror. "What's the first one? In the book, I mean. The first lie he tells us."

Francesca flipped backward, unbothered, the way she was unbothered by most things, including his arrival. "Depends what you count. He says he's just going to tell you about this one crazy Christmas and not his whole life, and then he can't even do that. He keeps drifting." She found a page near the start and turned the book so he could see the highlighted line. "But there's this. Early on. He flat out tells you."

Luke read it. In The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, the narrator Holden Caulfield tells readers, "I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life." He read it twice, because it seemed like a trick. A liar announcing himself, in his own account, in the first chapter, before the lying had even gotten going. It was like the cashier telling you the register was short.

"He just says it," Luke said. "Right to us."

"Right to us," Francesca agreed. "So the question is what you do with that. That's what my sister's college professor apparently asked her class."

"Do we throw out everything after?"

"Do you throw out everything after?" She said it like she genuinely wanted to know, which sensitized him to the difference between being questioned and being asked. Teachers questioned. This was something else.

Adriano drifted back and hung over the seat. "What are you two doing?"

"Homework," Luke said.

"On the bus."

"The bus is munificent with time," Francesca said, gesturing at the forty remaining minutes of route, and Adriano looked at her the way people look at weather.

Luke worked it out loud, because that was the only way he had. "Okay. So there's one way to read it. He's a liar, so we can't trust anything, so the book is just him performing for us and we should hold the whole thing at arm's length." He paused. "Then there's the other way. He's the only one telling us anything. There's no other version. So if we don't trust him, we've got nothing, and the book knows that, and it's making us pick."

"Or," Francesca said, "he tells you he's a liar because he's the only honest thing he ever does, and then goes on lying anyway, and the point is you can't sort them. Some of it's true and you don't get to know which parts."

The bus went over the tracks by the hardware store and everyone's books lifted slightly off their laps, Holden's included, like the whole class rising to object.

"I hate that," Luke said. "I want to be able to say which."

"I know," Francesca said. She closed the book but kept her thumb in it, ungraciously, like a bookmark she hadn't paid for. "Ms. Mercado is going to love your essay either way."

"That's what worries me." He looked at the prompt again. Whose version. He thought about the way Holden called everyone a phony while performing for an audience he claimed not to care about, and about how the narrator of a book is a kind of liar by trade, since even an honest one is invented, and antiquity had been inventing them for as long as there had been books at all, which was either comforting or not. He could not decide. He wrote on the back of the prompt: he tells us himself, then asks us to stay anyway.

"That's not a thesis," Adriano said, reading over his shoulder.

"It's a start of one."

The bus slowed for his stop. Luke folded the paper back into his pocket, and Francesca held the paperback out to him.

"Take it," she said. "The tabs will confuse you, and that's good for you."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
Hayden had claimed the reading nook by the window because it was the only place in the house where the lamp worked and the Wi-Fi didn't, and tonight he needed both failures. On his lap sat a battered copy of Jane Eyre, flagged with torn Post-its, and beside it Ms. Kovalenko's photocopied handout on critical lenses, which began with the intimidating instruction to choose one and be ruthless about it. Monday's seminar required him to read a passage through a Marxist or a feminist lens, and he had spent forty minutes trying to decide which one would make him sound intelligent, which was not the same as thinking.

Olivier arrived at six with a bag of pretzels and no shame about eating them over Hayden's book. He dropped into the window seat and picked up the handout as though it might bite. "Feminist lens on Jane Eyre," he said. "That's the obvious one. She marries the guy and goes blind, or he does. One of them does."

"Both of those sentences are wrong," Hayden said. "He goes blind. She marries him anyway. That's the problem. If I use the feminist lens, I have to argue that she's either liberated or domesticated, and I don't think it's that simple."

Olivier tore open the pretzels with his teeth. "Then dichotomize less. You keep splitting everything into two options like there's a law."

There was a knock, and Malaya let herself in, holding her father's paperback of the Communist Manifesto with both hands, the way people hold things they expect to be confiscated. "My dad says if we're doing the Marxist lens we should actually read it. Not just a summary from a study website." She flipped to the first page, squinted, and read aloud: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. That's the opening of the first section. 1848. Marx and Engels just say it, like they're announcing the weather."

Olivier chewed for a while. "Does that fit Jane Eyre, though? She's a governess. She's not exactly storming anything."

Hayden pulled the novel back toward himself and found the passage he'd flagged, the one where Jane, starving and begging on the moors, is taken in by the Rivers family and immediately asked whether she is a servant or a lady, because the household cannot decide how to treat a woman it cannot classify. He read it out loud. The room got quieter than three people eating pretzels usually allows.

"That's it," Malaya said. "They can't place her, so they can't be polite to her correctly. Her whole problem in the book is that she's an orphan with a gentlewoman's education and no money. She's between classes. She's stuck in the gap."

"An interregnum," Hayden said, mostly to himself. "Between two reigns. She's not gentry and she's not a servant, and everyone around her panics because they don't know which rules apply." He wrote it down, then crossed out two earlier attempts. "But that's the Marxist reading. If I follow it all the way, her marriage to Rochester is her escaping the gap, and the inheritance is what makes the escape possible. Money, not love. Which is depressing but honestly kind of true."

Malaya raised the Manifesto like a referee's card. "Except the class-struggles line says history is all struggle. Jane's not struggling against a class exactly, she's just trying not to starve with dignity. Is that the same thing?"

"Maybe the struggle doesn't have to be a revolution," Olivier said. "Maybe it can be one governess being canny about who she lets sign her paycheck. She refuses St. John, she refuses being Rochester's mistress, she only marries Rochester when she's equal to him. That's her fighting, just quietly, in a way nobody would call fighting."

Hayden looked at the handout again, the instruction to choose one lens and be ruthless. He had wanted a system that would settle the book for him, the way a lens supposedly settles everything, and instead he had a Marxist reading that explained the money and left the marriage half-lit, and a feminist reading that explained the marriage and left the money in shadow. He wrote at the top of his page: both lenses, one passage, and a margin note that simply said unresolved, which he underlined twice, and then, feeling honest, three times.

"Your seminar's going to be a mess," Olivier said, pleased about it.

"It's going to be an honest mess," Hayden said. He read the line about class struggles aloud once more, quietly, testing it against Jane starving on the doorstep of a house full of people who couldn't decide what she was. Malaya reached over and took a pretzel without asking, the way only a friend of eleven years can, and Olivier turned the lamp on and off twice, uselessly, to see if the Wi-Fi would come back.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of 1 over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, which fills the one gap the power rule leaves.
story:
The bell over the door of the corner store had a cracked note to it, a flat clang that Anna had never gotten used to in all the afternoons she'd spent at the wobbly table by the slushie machine. She spread her notebook flat between two rings of condensation and waited for Sylvia, who came through the door at four minutes past four, shaking rain off her jacket.

"You said you'd help me," Sylvia said, dropping into the chair. "Ms. Zhu's exam is Friday and I don't get any of it. Not the stupid curves, not the area, none of it."

"You get more than you think," Anna said, which was the kind of thing a tutor was supposed to say, and which she did not entirely believe. She turned the notebook so Sylvia could see the page. "Okay. So the whole idea of the integral is area under a curve. You want the area between the curve and the x axis, between two points. That's it. That's the entire cathedral."

"That's not it, because then there's the antiderivative, and the antiderivative is where I die."

Anna tapped the first problem, a clean parabola, and walked her through it: the power rule, adding one to the exponent, dividing by the new exponent, evaluating at the top and bottom of the interval. Sylvia actually smiled when the number came out. "That wasn't so bad," she admitted.

"Here's the bad one," Anna said, and slid the next problem across. One over x, integrated from one to four. She watched Sylvia raise the exponent to zero, divide by zero, and freeze with her pencil hovering over the paper like something stunned.

"You can't divide by zero," Sylvia said. Her voice went querulous, high and complaining, the voice of someone who suspects the universe of cheating. "The rule just breaks. Is it a trick question?"

Behind the counter, Jacey was titrating syrup into the slushie machine, pouring in a thin red thread and counting under her breath, and Anna envied the plainness of it, the way the machine told you when you were done. She looked at the broken problem and felt the same vertigo she'd felt a week ago, sitting in the back of Ms. Zhu's class with her own exam face down on the desk.

"It's not a trick," Anna said slowly. "It's a hole. The power rule has one gap in it, and this problem is standing right in the gap." She turned to a blank page. Her father, who fixed engines, liked to say that every system has a part it can't fix itself, that you have to carry a spare. She had rolled her eyes at him for years. She drew the curve of one over x, then shaded the region beneath it with the side of her pencil, the graphite going silvery and soft.

"What happens if you just try the logarithm," she said, half to herself. "Not the power rule. The natural log."

"That's random," Sylvia said.

"Maybe." Anna wrote ln of x, evaluated it at four and at one, and subtracted. The pencil moved, the arithmetic assembled itself, and there it was, a number, sitting on the page as though it had been waiting. She checked it twice. She looked up the hallway of what she remembered from class, the afternoon Ms. Zhu had written something on the board while Anna was still turned around digging for a pen, the moment she had missed.

"The antiderivative of one over x is the natural log of the absolute value of x," Anna said, copying it out in careful letters. "Absolute value, because of negative x. It fills the one gap the power rule leaves. That's the spare part." She slid it toward Sylvia. "Everything else, you climb with the power rule. This one, you go around it."

Sylvia squinted at the line, then at her own ruined attempt, then back. "So when the exponent would be zero. When it's one over x. That's when it's a log."

"That's when it's a log."

Sylvia did the next three problems without looking up, and Anna watched her, and only then, in the quiet, did she take her own exam out of her backpack, the one she'd carried folded into the side pocket for a week, the one with the red 71 at the top and the same problem circled twice. She unfolded it and laid it on the table between them.

"I failed this," Anna said. "That exact problem. I divided by zero and then I just left it blank and sat there for twenty minutes." Sylvia looked at her, and Anna kept her voice even, because it was strange how the failure had turned out to be useful, how she could teach the gap only because she had fallen into it, and how she still couldn't decide whether that made the 71 worth something or whether she was just dressing up a hole. "Ms. Zhu lets you retake one exam a semester. Mine's Monday."

"Then you'd better do it again," Sylvia said, and spun the notebook back around, and pointed her pencil at the shaded region under the curve. "Show me the area one more time, from the top."

Jacey called from the counter that the cherry was running again, and the bell over the door clanged its flat note as somebody came in for milk. Anna picked up her pencil.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was based on only twelve children.
story:
Evan had the two articles side by side on the library table, both flagged with orange sticky notes, and neither of them would agree with the other. The first was a Danish cohort study, dense with tables, following an enormous population of children. The second was the notorious one, Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet, and Evan kept returning to its opening page as if the number there might change if he looked away and came back.

He was supposed to write a critical review comparing how each had approached the same question, and Mr. Greco had been clear in class that the essay was not about picking a winner. "Anyone can declare a verdict," he had said. "I want to see how you weigh them." That instruction had seemed generous at the time and now felt like being handed a rope with both ends missing.

Alexandra arrived at ten past three with her bag already open, sat down without greeting him, and pulled out her laptop. She was doing the same assignment with a different pair of articles, something about early literacy programs, and they had an arrangement: forty minutes of silent work, then they traded paragraphs. Evan watched her type for a while, then looked back at his own screen, where the cursor blinked at the end of a sentence he no longer believed in.

The sentence said that the Wakefield paper's conclusions had been undermined by later research, which was true, but it had also been true before the later research, and Evan could not stop noticing why. He read the methods section again, slowly, the way Mr. Greco had told them to, following the numbers rather than the conclusions. He counted on his finger under the table.

"Twelve," he said out loud, before he could stop himself.

Alexandra looked over. "Twelve what?"

"Twelve kids." He turned his screen toward her. "That's all he had. The whole paper, the one that started everything, it was based on twelve children." He tapped the page of the Danish study beside it. "And this one followed over half a million. It's not even a comparison. It's like weighing a raindrop against a lake."

She considered both screens with the particular patience she reserved for other people's discoveries. "So your review basically writes itself."

"No. That's the problem." He pulled the laptop back. "If I just say the small study is bad and the big study is good, I'm grading them on arithmetic. But there are things the big study can't do either. It averages everything out. It can tell you what happens across half a million children and it can't tell you anything about any single one of them." He heard how it sounded, like he was defending the indefensible, and maybe he was, a little, in the way Mr. Greco seemed to want defended: not the conclusion but the logic of comparison itself.

Alexandra was noncommittal. "Sounds like your essay, not mine." She went back to typing, and Evan went back to drafting, and for a while the library held only the sound of keys and the low hum of the radiators and the murmur of two freshmen at the circulation desk arguing about a fine.

He wrote three paragraphs. In the first he laid out what each study claimed and how. In the second he laid out the evidence, and here the number twelve did its work without needing him to shout about it; he simply placed the sample sizes in adjacent sentences and let the reader feel the drop. In the third he tried to say what remained unsettled, which was harder, because admitting uncertainty felt like admitting weakness, and he had been raised, schoolwise, on the opposite faith. Somewhere in the middle of the third paragraph he deleted a sentence about how a single striking result could transmute, in the public mind, into settled fact, and then he typed it back in, because it was the truest thing he had.

Mr. Greco came by near the end of the period, hands in his pockets, reading over shoulders without asking, which was apparently a librarian's privilege now that he had taken over the library along with the senior seminar. Evan minimized his draft instinctively, then un-minimized it, deciding in the same motion that hiding it was worse than showing it unfinished.

Mr. Greco read for a long moment. "This line here," he said, tapping the screen without touching it. "'The large study answers the question, but only the question it asked.' You sure you want to keep that?"

"I think so," Evan said. "It's the part I'm least sure about, so it seemed like the part I should say."

Mr. Greco's face gave nothing away, which Evan was learning might be its own kind of approval, or might not be. "Word count's due Friday." He moved on toward the freshmen.

When Alexandra swapped paragraphs with him at the agreed hour, she read his three pages without expression, then slid them back. "It's good," she said. "It's also the most hedge-filled thing I've ever read from you."

"That's the point," Evan said, and started gathering the articles, stacking the Wakefield paper on top. It was the thinner one, of course, barely twelve pages, and he noticed as he squared the pile that it felt heavier in his hand than the Danish study with its hundred and fifty pages of tables, which was obviously impossible, and which he decided not to mention, since Alexandra would only tell him he was imagining it. He put both in his bag, heavier on top.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Matthew had mixed the gray himself, titanium white with a whisper of black, and he had mixed enough of it to cover the whole sky in one go. He was painting the view from his grandmother's kitchen window, the one with the water tower and the long gray roof of the hardware store, because she had asked for something of the neighborhood before she moved out of it. The problem appeared in the second hour. On the left side of the canvas, where the sky sat above the orange brick of the building opposite, the gray looked almost pink, almost warm. On the right, above the hardware store's corrugated metal, the same gray went flat and cold, faintly blue. He had not touched either passage since the first coat. He stood back with his brush dripping and stared until his mother called up that the kettle was on.

He checked the palette first. The blob of gray was uniform; he dragged a clean knife through it and pressed a smear onto a scrap of white board, and the smear looked the same everywhere. Then he held the scrap beside the brick section and beside the metal section, and there, on a piece of board no bigger than a playing card, the gray shifted again, warm near the orange, cool near the blue-gray of the tin. He carried the scrap downstairs without wiping his hands and set it on the kitchen table next to his mother's crossword.

"It's the same paint," he said. "Same tube, same mix, same everything. It changes depending on where I put it."

His mother looked at the scrap, then at his face, and seemed to decide that this was not a riddle he was testing her with. She suggested, almost apologetically, that maybe he was tired. He wanted to disabuse her of that gently, because he had spent the whole morning wanting to disabuse himself of it, and had failed. The paint moved. He carried the scrap back up like evidence.

He texted Annalise, who was taking a gap semester and worked at the art supply store on Delancey. She answered with a photo of a shelf and the words come in before six. When he got there she was restocking brushes and Parsa was already there, sitting on a stool by the register, allegedly helping. Parsa was halfway through a degree in chemistry and treated every question as a personal provocation.

"The gray looks different on different parts of the canvas," Matthew said. "Same gray."

Annalise pulled down a book from behind the counter, a fat paperback with a cracked spine, color reproductions of squares nested inside squares. She flopped it open to a page she had clearly been to before. "Somebody already had your problem," she said. "He wrote it up." She tapped the caption. "A chemist. Michel Eugène Chevreul. He ran the dye works at a tapestry factory, and the weavers kept blaming the dyers for colors that weren't wrong."

Parsa leaned over. "Chevreul," he said. "The law of simultaneous contrast. 1839." He said it the way he said everything, as though the fact had been sitting in his head for years waiting for someone to need it. "A color appears to shift toward the complement of the color next to it. So your gray next to orange goes blue, and your gray next to blue-gray looks warm." He flipped through the plates: a gray bar on red, the same gray bar on green, two grays that anyone would swear were different paints.

Matthew read the page twice. It was not exactly reassuring. His whole plan had been that the sky would be one thing, uniform, and the buildings another, and the picture would hold together by keeping its parts clean. Now the parts were talking to each other whether he wanted them to or not. He said as much, and Parsa shrugged and said that was true of everything, paint and people both, though Matthew suspected the second half of that sentence was tangential, an excuse for Parsa to sound profound on a stool.

He sat on the floor of the store with the book and a piece of grayboard Annalise cut for him, and he tried small studies. If he let the bricks go slightly duller, the sky above them calmed down. If he warmed the metal roof a touch, the right side of the sky stopped looking like evening. He could not make both passages agree, not exactly, but he could aim the disagreement. That was the part he turned over on the bus home. His grandmother would see the painting through her own kitchen window, which sat above a different wall, under a different light, and the sky he made tonight would not be the sky she saw. Everything he made would keep drifting a little, the way his grandmother said her apartment already drifted toward disorder no matter how often she tidied it. She had a word for that, entropy, picked up from a documentary, and she used it about the apartment, about the neighborhood, about all of them.

At home he mixed a fresh batch of gray, a little warmer than the last, and set his grandmother's chair by the window where she would sit for it. He taped the study to the easel's edge. Then he loaded the brush and started on the bricks.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Maxime had signed up because the form said the food bank needed hands, and it turned out the food bank, this branch of it, lived in the common room of a seniors' residence on the far side of town, where folding tables had been pushed together under a banner reading Thursday Distribution. He arrived fifteen minutes early, which felt like the only credential he had. A girl from his old school, Lilianne, was already there, sorting cans into rows, and she waved him over with a jar of peanut butter in each hand.

"You're on intake with me," she said. "Mostly it's residents, but some people come in from the neighbourhood. You take the name, mark the box, no big speeches."

There was a poster taped to the wall behind the tables, curling at one corner, and while Lilianne went to find tape he read it to have something to do with his eyes. The first food bank in the world, it said, was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, founded in 1967 by a man named John van Hengel. He read it twice, because 1967 sounded wrong to him, too recent somehow, and then he realized he had never once wondered where the idea had come from. He had assumed food banks were like weather, just a condition of the world.

"Did you know that?" he asked Lilianne when she came back. "Phoenix, 1967. A guy named John van Hengel started the whole thing."

She glanced at the poster. "That's why it's up there," she said, not unkindly. "Hold this crate."

The doors opened at four. The work was simpler and harder than he had expected. An old man who introduced himself as Mr. Rao came through with a wheeled walker and a precise, silent system: he pointed at what he wanted, Maxime bagged it, and neither of them wasted a word. Maxime found he liked this. Mr. Rao was taciturn in a way that didn't feel like coldness, more like a man who had decided long ago what was worth saying, and had been right about it.

Then a woman arrived who was not on the list. She was younger than the residents, maybe forty, holding a bus transfer and no bag, and she said she'd moved in with her mother last week, in 3B, after a hospital stay, and she needed food for both of them while she convalesced. Lilianne's pen stopped over the clipboard. The rules, she said quietly, were that the mother had to come herself, or there had to be a note, some proof of address. It wasn't Lilianne's rule. She hated saying it; Maxime could see that in her shoulders.

"That's a contrivance," Maxime said, not loudly, when the woman had stepped aside to phone her mother. "The rule, I mean. It's not about anyone's actual hunger. It's paperwork wearing a costume."

"It's so people don't take what isn't theirs," Lilianne said. "We only have what we have."

He didn't have an answer ready. He looked down the table and saw that Mr. Rao had stopped at the far end and was watching, one hand resting on the walker, waiting with his usual patience. Maxime excused himself, bagged Mr. Rao's pasta and tinned pears and the small carton of milk, and while he did it he kept turning the problem over. The rule existed because the food was scarce, not because the woman was lying. But the woman was standing in the hallway with a bus transfer in her hand, and hunger didn't queue for paperwork.

He went back and found the woman still on the phone, and behind her, coming slowly down the corridor with her own cane, an elderly woman in a cardigan, breathless, saying, "I'm here, I'm here, you didn't have to call me out, but I'm here."

Lilianne looked at the two of them, then at her clipboard, then wrote something and turned the board around so Maxime could see it: two names, two boxes ticked. "Don't get used to it," she said, but she was already reaching for a second bag.

When the line had thinned, Maxime carried the crates to the storeroom and passed the poster again. Phoenix, 1967, one man, John van Hengel. Somebody had looked at surplus on one side and hunger on the other and decided the problem was the distance between them. The rules Lilianne defended and the ones he'd argued against were both attempts to keep that bridge from collapsing under too many feet, and he still didn't know which of them was more nearly right, or whether the question even had a right answer, only better and worse afternoons.

On his way out, Mr. Rao was waiting by the doors. He lifted one hand from the walker, deliberately, and held it out. "Thursday," Mr. Rao said. "Same table?"

"Same table," Maxime said, and shook the old man's hand.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The room smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's dusty heat, and Eva had claimed the desk by the window because the light there made her graph paper look almost blue. Math club met on Thursdays in Mr. Gill's classroom, twelve of them and a tin of shortbread that Marek's grandmother sent, and today the whiteboard said, in Mr. Gill's looping hand, DERIVATIVES AND MAXIMA. Eva had been waiting for this all week, though she would not have said so out loud.

"I want the actual rule," she had told Eleanor back in September, on the day she'd almost quit the club entirely. That was the flashback that kept surfacing whenever she got stuck: the two of them on the bleachers in September, Eleanor pulling her sleeves over her hands, saying that math club was full of people who liked being right more than they liked anything else. "You're turning into a misanthrope," Eleanor had said, and Eva had answered that she wasn't, she just wanted one place where being right meant something clean, where you could prove a thing and it stayed proved. She had stayed. Eleanor had gone off to debate instead, and they still ate lunch together, but it was never quite the same.

Now Mr. Gill set them a problem: a farmer with six hundred meters of fence, a rectangular pen against a river, and the question of the largest area the fence could enclose. Marek was across from her, already writing. Marek was fast the way water is fast, all downhill, and Eva watched him derive the area function, set its derivative equal to zero, and announce the answer before anyone else had finished copying the problem.

"Width one hundred fifty, length three hundred, area forty-five thousand square meters," he said. "The derivative's zero there, so that's the maximum. Done."

Eeva looked down at her own page. Her polynomial was the same as his, and her derivative was the same, and she had found the same zero. But something snagged in her, a habit Eleanor used to tease her about, the tendency to problematize a finished thing, to turn it over and ask what it was resting on. Because between last week and this week there had been a Tuesday afternoon, alone in the library, when she had tried to sketch a function just for the pleasure of its shape. She had picked x cubed. She had differentiated it, gotten three x squared, watched it vanish at x equals zero, and drawn what she expected: a little hill at the origin. But when she plotted the points, negative one, then zero, then one, the curve did not hill at all. It went up, flattened for one breathless instant at the origin, and went on rising. The derivative was zero at x equals zero, and there was no maximum there, no minimum either, nothing but the graph sailing straight through its own flat moment.

She had sat with that for a long time, feeling something shift. She had not told anyone about it, not even Eleanor, mostly because she did not know yet what it meant.

"Marek," she said now. "What if the zero doesn't give you the top?"

"It always gives you the top. Wherever the derivative is zero, that's the max. That's the whole rule."

She pulled a clean sheet toward her. "Graph it first," she said, and drew axes, then the river pen, width along one axis and area along the other, plotting the area function at width fifty, one hundred, one hundred fifty, two hundred. The area climbed, peaked exactly where the derivative had gone quiet, and fell away after. So for this function, Marek's shortcut had landed on truth. She plotted a second function beside it, small, in the corner: x cubed, its derivative zero at the origin, its graph rising through that point with no maximum anywhere in sight.

"Look," she said, and turned the sheet so he could see both. "A zero derivative doesn't guarantee a maximum or a minimum. X cubed has derivative zero at x equals zero, and the graph just keeps rising through that point." She tapped the corner sketch, then the farmer's curve. "Your answer's right, but not because of the reason you said."

Marek leaned in, chewing the last of a shortbread. Mr. Gill had drifted over and was reading the sheet upside down with his hands behind his back, saying nothing, which for Mr. Gill was a kind of applause. The window darkened slightly as a cloud crossed, and the lugubrious light made the two graphs on Eva's page look like a single landscape, one hill and one long steady climb.

"So the rule is broken," Marek said.

"The rule is smaller than you thought it was," Eva said. "The flat spot is where a maximum might be. Then you have to look." It occurred to her that this was the opposite of what she'd told Eleanor on the bleachers, the clean proved thing that stays proved. She examined the feeling and found she didn't mind. She was seventeen; she was allowed to keep both positions for a while and see which one held weight. She still wasn't sure whether certainty was something you found or something you built out of checks, and she supposed she'd find out in some classroom or other over the next few years.

"Okay," Marek said, taking out a fresh pencil. "Then I'll check the values on either side. Width one forty, one fifty, one sixty."

"Start a new sheet," Eva said, and slid the graph paper across to him.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Gottfried Leibniz introduced the integral sign in 1675, basing it on an elongated letter s because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum.
story:
The community centre had one warm room and the rest were boreal in the way of old buildings, cold that came up through the tiles and settled in the ankles, so Stella kept her boots on while she spread her notes across the table by the window. Tuesday was math tutoring. She had signed up to help, which was a strange thing given that she was also there to be helped, though no one at the centre knew both halves of that arrangement except her.

Zainab arrived first, as always, dropping her bag on the chair opposite and pulling out a worksheet covered in slopes and limits. Then Kate, sixteen and grudging, sent by a mother who had remonstrated with the centre's coordinator until a slot was found. Kate was the reason Stella had started studying calculus at eleven at night, because Kate's questions were the sharp kind, and Stella had learned quickly that a tutor who says "let me check on that" three times in a row stops being believed.

Tonight's worksheet had curves on it, and beneath the curves, that new symbol, tall and narrow and curved like a wire stretched almost straight. Kate squinted at it and put her pencil down.

"Why does it look like that," she said. "Like somebody pulled a letter too far."

Stella opened her mouth, and nothing came. She knew what the symbol did, roughly. She knew it meant adding up, area, all the thin slices under a curve, but she had never once asked where the shape itself had come from, and the question made her feel the way a missing stair makes you feel in the dark.

"Give me a minute," she said, and walked to the shelf of abandoned books near the radiator, where the centre kept a decade of donated textbooks nobody taught from anymore. The third one she pulled down had a water-stained cover and, tucked in a chapter called something dry about notation, a paragraph that stopped her with her finger pressed flat against it.

Gottfried Leibniz had introduced the integral sign in 1675. He had based it on an elongated letter s, because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum. She read it twice, standing there with the cold coming up through her boots, and something in her chest loosened and tightened at once, because a year ago she had stood in a different cold place, in the corridor outside her old school's math office, holding a withdrawal form for the calculus course she had signed up for with such confidence in September. She had told everyone she dropped it because of scheduling. She had told her father it was scheduling. The boreal dark had been pressing on the windows of that corridor too, and she had watched her reflection in the glass decide, in the space of about four seconds, to become a person who had never really tried.

She carried the book back to the table.

"It's a stretched letter s," she told Kate. "Leibniz made it that way in 1675, because he thought of an integral as an infinite sum. Sum, s. Like the letter got pulled long to hold all of it."

Kate looked at the symbol again, and her face did the thing faces do when something arbitrary suddenly has a reason. "That's it? That's the whole story?"

"That's the whole story," Stella said, and it was true, and it also wasn't, because she could feel the rest of it crowding up behind her teeth.

Zainab was watching her with a careful expression. Zainab had been at the old school. Zainab had seen the withdrawal form, or heard about it, or guessed; Stella had never known which, and had never asked, because asking would mean admitting there was something to ask about. The room ticked with the radiator. Outside, somebody's car doors slammed in the parking lot.

"There's something I should say," Stella said. "About why I'm good at the tutoring questions lately." She turned the water-stained book so Zainab could see the page, the elongated s, the date. "I dropped calculus last year. That form I made you think was about scheduling. I've been relearning it at midnight so I could stay ahead of you two, which is a stupid way to learn anything, treating your own gaps like some externality you can push onto nobody and ignore." She heard her voice go thin and kept going anyway. "The area under the curve is just the sum of slices. The slices I skipped are still under there."

Kate had picked her pencil back up. She drew the integral sign once, slowly, elongated, careful, on the corner of her worksheet, the way you draw something to remember it. Zainab still hadn't said anything, and the radiator ticked, and Stella slid the open book across the table toward her.
